Um so we had a couple of uh updates and so uh the first one is around the metro rapid response funding and so uh we will have uh Amoris Gomez who will uh present and then uh open up for any questions that we may have. >> Good morning. My name is Amoris Gomez and I am the landlord engagement manager for the office of homeless services. Thank you for the opportunity to speak to you today. I will be presenting on the Metro Rapid Response Fund Pilot, also known as MURF. I know there are a lot of questions around it, so hopefully my very lengthy presentation answers some of that for you. The um so [clears throat] again, MetroRapid Response, also known as MURF, is designed to strengthen our homelessness response system through the diversion approach that helps individuals and families access housing more quickly before their homelessness becomes prolonged and more difficult to resolve. There is a there was a conversation, I know, with the executive committee and the suggestions that were made have been considered and incorporated within the MURF document. So, thank you. The purpose of MURF is to address a gap in our current housing system. Many HUDF funded homelessness programs prioritize individuals experiencing chronic homelessness, often with those co-occurring conditions. While this prioritization is necessary, it can leave individuals and families who are newly homeless without timely access to housing resources. Households who may not score highly on the vulnerability assessment often remain on housing list for an extended period even though they are still at a significant risk of prolonged homelessness. So MURF creates a local pathway that provides assistance sooner, helping prevent short-term housing crisis from beginning from becoming long-term homelessness situations. And the goal of MURF is very simple. that is to move into housing faster and test whether earlier intervention leads to a stronger long-term outcome and prevent the return to homelessness. By preparing short-term rental assistance, I'm sorry, by pairing short-term rental assistance with intensive case management that is provided by our community partners. MURF shortens the time households spend unhoused, reduce exposure to trauma associated with homelessness, creates a pathway toward long-term housing stability, and prevents the return to homelessness. This pilot allows us to evaluate whether earlier investment improves long-term outcomes for households and strengthens the overall homelessness response system. Now, all individuals that are referred to MURF must be considered housing ready, meaning that they have the essential documents and income needed to secure and sustain permanent housing using a targeted universalism approach. The specific subop currently prioritized in this p pilot include people experiencing unsheltered homelessness, families in emergency shelters, and veterans experiencing literal homelessness. These groups have been a continued focus within our community. However, some households may not score high enough on the coordinated entry assessment to quickly receive referrals for housing programs. Households that are housing ready are most likely to benefit from the short-term assistance and successfully uh be remade housed. MURF provides a flexible financial assistance to address immediate barriers that prevent households from securing housing. Financial assistance includes rental aars, security deposits, first month's rent, ongoing rental subsidies, and utility assistance. By addressing these financial needs quickly, we are able to help households access housing faster and be stabilized more quickly. Because MURF is a pilot, uh at the moment, we are focused on measuring outcomes directly tied to financial assistance. This allows us to evaluate what is working based on our local investment. We access housing. I'm sorry. We assess housing stability by looking at whether the participants are moving into housing and achieving stability faster, achieving self-sufficiency and paying rent, assessing other long-term rental uh subsidies, and remaining hous and avoiding return to homelessness. Uh research on the rapid rehousing and diversion focused interventions consistently show that financial assistance reduces the return to homelessness and lowers long-term costs in the broader system. Once again, we are continuing to evaluate the outcomes and refine the approach as we learn what strategies are most effective. We do not yet have all the answers and we are hopeful that this pilot will provide a valuable insight. Now at this time we cannot project a deadline for when the pilot will become complete um as uh ongoing evaluation is essential to understand the long-term effectiveness. Currently, OHS has received 91 MURF referrals and of those 40 households have been successful in securing housing and 51 are actively working with OS staff and case managers to identify housing, complete lease applications, and overcome barriers within their placement. At this time, the referrals are made through OHS street outreach teams, emergency family shelters, and the Department of Veteran Affairs. What makes this pilot different is that it introduces an alternative local prioritization pathway. As I previously mentioned, this allows Metro to serve households who may not score high enough for HUDf funed programs, but will still be provided with immediate housing intervention. This diversion strategy creates flexibility for Metro to address barriers that contribute to longer stays in homelessness and provide financial assistance that prevent the return to homelessness. By helping individuals and families move into sustainable housing more quickly, the demand for emergency assistance decreases. This helps relieve pressure across the homeless response system, including coordinated entries, emergency shelters, and other metro departments. Now, in closing, the Metro Rapid Response Fund pilot provides a flexible, locally responsive tool that allows us to assist in assist households earlier before their homelessness becomes prolonged. By removing the immediate financial barriers and providing targeted support, MURF helps households secure stable housing faster and strengthens the overall effectiveness in our homelessness response system. We are hopeful that this pilot will provide meaningful insight into how early intervention can improve long-term housing outcomes. I will be presenting on the Metro Rapid Response Fund Pilot, also known as MURF. I know there are a lot of questions around it, so hopefully my very lengthy presentation answers some of that for you. The um so [clears throat] again, MetroRapid Response, also known as MURF, is designed to strengthen our homelessness response system through the diversion approach that helps individuals and families access housing more quickly before their homelessness becomes prolonged and more difficult to resolve. There is a there was a conversation, I know, with the executive committee and the suggestions that were made have been considered and incorporated within the MURF document. So, thank you. The purpose of MURF is to address a gap in our current housing system. Many HUDF funded homelessness programs prioritize individuals experiencing chronic homelessness, often with those co-occurring conditions. While this prioritization is necessary, it can leave individuals and families who are newly homeless without timely access to housing resources. Households who may not score highly on the vulnerability assessment often remain on housing list for an extended period even though they are still at a significant risk of prolonged homelessness. So MURF creates a local pathway that provides assistance sooner, helping prevent short-term housing crisis from beginning from becoming long-term homelessness situations. And the goal of MURF is very simple. that is to move into housing faster and test whether earlier intervention leads to a stronger long-term outcome and prevent the return to homelessness. By preparing short-term rental assistance, I'm sorry, by pairing short-term rental assistance with intensive case management that is provided by our community partners. MURF shortens the time households spend unhoused, reduce exposure to trauma associated with homelessness, creates a pathway toward long-term housing stability, and prevents the return to homelessness. This pilot allows us to evaluate whether earlier investment improves long-term outcomes for households and strengthens the overall homelessness response system. Now, all individuals that are referred to MURF must be considered housing ready, meaning that they have the essential documents and income needed to secure and sustain permanent housing using a targeted universalism approach. The specific subop currently prioritized in this p pilot include people experiencing unsheltered homelessness, families in emergency shelters, and veterans experiencing literal homelessness. These groups have been a continued focus within our community. However, some households may not score high enough on the coordinated entry assessment to quickly receive referrals for housing programs. Households that are housing ready are most likely to benefit from the short-term assistance and successfully uh be remade housed. MURF provides a flexible financial assistance to address immediate barriers that prevent households from securing housing. Financial assistance includes rental aars, security deposits, first month's rent, ongoing rental subsidies, and utility assistance. By addressing these financial needs quickly, we are able to help households access housing faster and be stabilized more quickly. Because MURF is a pilot, uh at the moment, we are focused on measuring outcomes directly tied to financial assistance. This allows us to evaluate what is working based on our local investment. We access housing. I'm sorry. We assess housing stability by looking at whether the participants are moving into housing and achieving stability faster, achieving self-sufficiency and paying rent, assessing other long-term rental uh subsidies, and remaining hous and avoiding return to homelessness. Once again, we are continuing to evaluate the outcomes and refine the approach as we learn what strategies are most effective. We do not yet have all the answers and we are hopeful that this pilot will provide a valuable insight. Now at this time we cannot project a deadline for when the pilot will become complete um as uh ongoing evaluation is essential to understand the long-term effectiveness. What makes this pilot different is that it introduces an alternative local prioritization pathway. As I previously mentioned, this allows Metro to serve households who may not score high enough for HUDf funed programs, but will still be provided with immediate housing intervention. This diversion strategy creates flexibility for Metro to address barriers that contribute to longer stays in homelessness and provide financial assistance that prevent the return to homelessness. By helping individuals and families move into sustainable housing more quickly, the demand for emergency assistance decreases. This helps relieve pressure across the homeless response system, including coordinated entries, emergency shelters, and other metro departments. Now, in closing, the Metro Rapid Response Fund pilot provides a flexible, locally responsive tool that allows us to assist in assist households earlier before their homelessness becomes prolonged. Um All right. >> [clears throat] >> Good morning, Mr. Chair and members of the Homelessness Planning Council. I'm here to request a few small changes uh process changes in our meetings. Um when I look around this room, I see passionate, experienced people who care deeply about this work. What I do not see is a council operating with the urgency, structure, and accountability that this crisis demands. These meetings feel focused on bureaucratic process updates rather than outcomes, and it is difficult to identify what decisions were made, what barriers were addressed, what progress occurred since the last meeting, or who is responsible for the next steps. How are we moving the needle? For a body with limited time and significant responsibility, every agenda item should connect to system improvement, accountability, decision-making, or learning directly from people experiencing homelessness. For example, at the last meeting, instead of hearing from the chair or members of the Performance Evaluation Committee, we heard from an Office of Homeless Services employee. The result was hearing about the system rather than hearing from the committee charged with helping guide it. That distinction matters. I appreciate the OHS staff, but they're supposed to be facilitating this work based on your guidance, not running every aspect of it while you watch. As a community, we depend on this council to lead. We depend on each one of you to be proactive rather than reactive. We need to know what recommendations are being made, what obstacles are standing in the way, and how this body is using its authority to move the system forward. I'm talking about long-term progress. I can hear it in your conversations and see it in your commitment to this work. But, I also believe that frustration can be productive if it leads to action. These meetings should feel purposeful, accountable, and action-oriented. Members should leave knowing what changed, what remains unresolved, who owns the next step, and when progress will be reviewed again. With that in mind, I would respectfully request these few small process changes. Please require committee chairs or designated committee members to report progress, barriers, decisions needed, and next steps at every meeting. I'm glad to see a a few on the agenda for today. Please create more opportunities for people experiencing homelessness, service providers, and frontline workers to identify what is working and what is failing. And please I end every meeting with clearly identified action items, responsible parties, and follow-up expectations. Most importantly, continue bringing the conversation back to housing and the concrete actions required to move people into stable homes. I'm not sharing these comments to attack anyone. I'm sharing them because the stakes are too high. The Homelessness Planning Council occupies a unique position in our community. Few groups bring together this level of expertise, lived experience, and influence in one room. We can do this. docs.text: All right, it is 9 o'lock. Hopefully everyone is making it to their seat. I think you all have already found the restrooms, but if you haven't already, there are both men and women's restrooms located to the back of the room, the right and left of you. So, welcome, welcome everyone to the 2026 State of Homelessness Symposium. Many of you know me, but I'm going to introduce myself anyway. I am Demetrius Cheney. I'm the public information officer for the office of homeless services. It is an honor to have you in the room again this year. Raise your hand if you were here last year. Great, great, great. Raise your hand if you are new to the symposium experience. Well, welcome. Welcome. You picked a great year to be here. Um before we begin, I want to thank many leaders, partners, advocates, uh the mayor's office, Metro Council, our homelessness planning um council and chair, uh the continuum of care, the office of homeless services staff, service providers, community organizations, funders, advocates, and friends who have joined us today. Thank you so much for being here. Thank you for your partnership, your leadership, and your continued commitment to our neighbors experiencing homelessness. Before we begin, I want to acknowledge something that many of us have probably already thought about. If you um are here for the first time or if you are returning, why is this symposium like um a celebration of sorts when there are still so many people homeless? You may be wondering that and that is a very valid question. Here's the answer. We don't wait until every challenge is solved before we start recognizing the lives that have already been impacted by change. We don't wait until every funding stream ends before celebrating the partnerships that have already transformed our community. We don't wait until the work is finished to acknowledge the people like yourselves who've poured their time, expertise, and compassion into moving this work forward. Another thought, some of you may also be thinking, "The numbers in this report are static. In fact, they are already changing." You are exactly right. Since this report was printed, more people have been housed through flexible funding and housing programs. And you are also correct. More people have become homeless. This work continues. That reality feels uncomfortable, which is why we're here today. We want a clear finish line. And the truth is that every finish line in this work often becomes the starting point for the next challenge. How many of you agree with that? Yeah. Every person housed creates an opportunity to focus on the next person still waiting. Every success reveals where more work remains. And today you're going to hear about lots of successes. But what you'll also hear is there is so much opportunity for more to be done. So yes, today is about celebration, but more importantly, today is about holding that tension between homelessness and housing and working together as a com as a community to close the distance between the two. I will say that again. today is about holding that tension between homelessness and housing and working together as a community to close the distance between them. Thank you all for being here. We look forward to the work that we're going to do in this next and I will say in this next six months but also in this next year. So let's begin. Our first keynote speaker, Donald Whitehead Jr. is a nationally recognized advocate, policy leader, and person in long-term recovery. Having experienced homelessness firsthand, he has spent more than 25 years working to advance housing recovery and opportunities for people across the country. Today, he serves as the executive director of the National Coalition for the Homeless and is widely respected as one of the nation's leading voices on homelessness policy and lived experience. Please join us in welcoming Dr. Excuse me, Donald Whitehead Jr. Good morning. Thank you so much for being here. And off the top, I just want to say congratulations uh to the city of Nashville for joining the lawsuit to challenge uh the new policies that uh have been put in place by the administration. [applause] And uh it is really really important that uh we we stand uh because there is the the threat of maybe at least 97,000 people losing their housing just because of those changes. And I don't care who you voted for. We don't want to see 97,000 people who you've worked a hard hard to already house uh go back into the homeless population. So again, uh, I really appreciate you guys doing that. I want to just do a little framing to start things off. Uh, and then I'll get into the core message that I'd like for you to to have a little bit about our organization. I won't spend the whole time talking about us, but the National Coalition is the oldest and largest advocacy group that is uh, operated, directed, and led by people with lived experience. And if you don't know of us by name, you know of us by the deeds, you know of us by the work that we've done over the course of the last 40 years. Uh if you get resources from the McKenna Vento Act um uh or the education for homeless children and youth uh we were responsible for drafting and helping to introduce the McKenna Vento Act way back in 1987 and the education for homeless children and youth act in the early 2000s. Just a little framing of the issue. Um, again, we're a national organization, national network of people with lived experience, but not just people with lived experience. We also have in our midst providers, people of faith. Um, we have people who are in government right now. Uh, we have just a variety of people who every day dedicate themselves to making sure that people with lived experience have the opportunity to thrive. Now last year um we saw um an incredible increase in homelessness. It was actually the largest increase in the history of homelessness in this country. Uh there was an 18% increase the year before, a 12% increase for a 30% increase over the course of two years. Uh this year we saw a 3% or a little over 3% decrease. uh and there's two uh ways to think about that. One is that uh some of what we already have in place is working. So there is no need for a dramatic uh change in the way we do things as we see proposed right now. But we also know that some of that is due to things like criminalization. Uh people haven't been counted because they can't be found because they're hiding out because they don't want to get arrested. Um, so there there's reason for applause, but there's also uh there's also a need not to overreact to that. Um, we have seen homelessness remain steady uh over the course of the last 40 years. We we we've seen uh es and flows uh but for the most part uh we've managed homelessness. uh we've not gotten to the point of real change and that can only come by addressing the structural needs of homelessness. Okay, so I went through two really fast. Um so the the last slide was talking about families. Uh two years ago, uh the family growth and homelessness was 38%. Um and that was driven by increased housing cost. Uh a move back to evictions that was prior to COVID. You know in COVID we had the eviction moratorum. We slowly actually quickly went back to that number. And so now we have uh uh we've seen a decrease in national homelessness. And I won't get really into the weeds. I know uh my good friend Richard Cho will get into the weeds more later. So um but uh we did see uh a phenomenon that started to emerge a few years ago and continues today and that's the growth of people 55 years of age and older. So the majority of the people living unsheltered in America are 55 years of age and older and uh that should not happen in the richest country in the history of the world. Um these are just some timeline uh numbers provided by HUD that show you kind of the trajectory of homelessness over the last few years. Um and I won't go deep into that. Um this is actually the number of children. Uh and what you'll see there is that the way we count homelessness, and I won't get into uh needing to change the way we count homelessness, but uh the the education department, the National Education Association, uh says that there's about 3.5 million children that are homeless. And so, uh we know our point in time count is a one-time count uh at the um in January. and and there are a lot of people that get missed in that count, but there there's a lot of children. Um I said 3.5 is 1.37 million children um that are homeless in our school system in this country. So uh those are some numbers that estimate uh the unsheltered locations, emergency shelter, transitional housing. Uh you see the numbers in Tennessee. Uh they estimate about 8,000 people either in shelter or in one of those programs. uh and the percentages of people who are unhoused in jurisdictions are there you see Tennessee uh about 46% of the people according to the point in time count are unhoused uh so there are going to be some changes uh we know that the no if it doesn't get changed by this lawsuit uh there'll be limits on housing first uh we know that to be a uh solution that in in many places has a more than 80% success rate. Um we know that it's an effective strategy. Uh we know that a lot of changes that are being proposed uh will have a impact on people experiencing homelessness and programs in our community and I won't go through them one by one but uh there's a lot of conditions on housing. Uh there's work requirements. There's uh limits on people who come uh from mixed families, mixed immigration families. Uh there is uh uh an attack on fair housing. Uh actually that department's been decimated. And I could go on and on. There's a lot of changes uh that are in uh on the table for communities across the country. Uh and I again there's there's a lot of federal changes and the one thing you should know is it's not just HUD, it's across the federal government. So the executive order uh that the president presented back in February uh to kind of uh the law and order uh executive order is being utilized in the department of justice, the department of housing and human services and the department of head HUD. So across the board uh you see this push towards criminalization which we believe will have a devastating impact on people experiencing homelessness and programs. Um so I won't go again through all the different um uh places but you know there's work requirements. Uh there's um the the proposed changes as I mentioned to uh the supportive housing program. There's also time limits in subsidized housing. So uh from two to five years uh would be your lifetime in public housing programs. uh and that alone could cause uh millions of people to become homeless. So uh the time limits themselves would uh cause the potential of 3 million people becoming homeless including 1.7 million children. Now they might not become homeless right away. Uh they might find family members. They might find uh the payby-week hotels. Uh that's the trajectory that you normally see. but it it could have a devastating impact on housing. Uh we hope to push against that as well. And here's just some numbers from Tennessee. Uh so we we see in Tennessee that the available affordable housing per 100 renters. Uh if you're at below or extremely low income, uh there's 39 units per 100 people. uh if you're in the 50% of area medium range, there's 59 units per 100 people. And you also see where people are costbururdened. Um and obviously you aren't as cost burdened if you're middle income or higher, but if you're at the lower end of that spectrum, uh you see how many people uh are costburdened here in Tennessee. And uh these slides are from the gap analysis uh the gap study by the national low-inccome housing coalition. They also do a study called um out of reach and it looks at what it actually cost uh to have housing in a given jurisdiction. Uh this particular um uh slide says that uh the minimum wage is is 725, but what it actually cost and and what it means is that you would only pay 30% of your income for housing. Um and that's what the federal government says you should be paying in order to do that and afford a two-bedroom housing unit in the state of Tennessee, you need to make about $27 an hour. Um, if you're working a minimum wage job, uh, you would have to work 129 hours to be able to afford a one-bedroom housing unit in the state of Tennessee. Uh, so the percentage of renters that are below that are 23% of the renters in your state. So, the reason we have growing homelessness um is is really rooted in the cost of housing in communities. And until we again address some of the structural issues, we'll continue to see that. So we also know that uh two years ago the Supreme Court decided that it was lawful to criminalize people because they were homeless. And um you know that some of those practices uh have uh really gone to the extreme. Uh in um 360 cities we've documented there's been new criminalization ordinances put in place. Uh some of the worst are right here in Tennessee where it's a felony. Uh if you're homeless on public property in Kentucky, they have a stand your ground law that says if they find you homeless and you're on someone's property, they can use force against you up to and including deadly force. And just recently, Louisiana passed a law that said um that you can be given a felony if you're homeless with two to five years in jail. And they also can um uh give you hard labor. Now, if you think about that for a minute, that is taking us all the way back to slave codes, to Jim Crow laws. Uh that was what they did with a fugitive slaves or or formerly enslaved people. Uh you were given hard labor and you were uh kind of given out to uh community organizations for work uh for free. And that's what is being suggested in Louisiana. So, uh, this is a lot more serious than you would think. So, just a little bit about what we do, and I'm going to be wrapping up and going into, uh, my my comments. Uh, the Bring America Home Now campaign is a campaign that we launched four years ago. Uh and what we're trying to do with that campaign is rebuild the movement that got us things like the McKenna Vento Act, uh low-income housing tax credits, the Cranston Gonzalez Act, and any almost any of the uh resources that we have available today. That didn't just come uh because uh they thought that people experiencing homelessness were good people. It came through protest and organizing. And so the bring America home is about that. Uh we don't want to manage homeless anymore, homelessness anymore. We want to actually get to the point where we're actually working to end it and not just managing it. And so we have uh 10 pieces of legislation that uh are part of that campaign. Affordable housing, homeless prevention, the decriminalization of poverty, ext expanded shelter standards. Uh we don't have standards in shelters in this country. So you can basically operate a shelter any way you want to. Uh we have employment programs. Uh we we want every program to have trauma-informed care. Uh treatment on demand. Uh we want to really look at how we uh manage people that are in in encampments. We want to make sure there's an infrastructure so people uh can uh actually go from those situations to housing. Uh we we want to get rid of all the dollars that are wasted on hostile architecture. And if you don't know what that is, the big boulders under the bridge or spikes under the bridge or a fence around a place where people were forced to stay. And then we also want to make sure that there's equity across the board uh between genders, races, uh and everybody else who might be involved. Uh we also have something that I hope you you'll take advantage of. It's our lived experience training academy. And that academy uh provides the opportunity for people with lived experience uh to be able to learn to become advocates because we think that uh the way we get to the point where we have enough people to make a difference when it comes to our elected officials uh is we have to train the people who are most affected. So this program is a 16-hour training. When people complete it, they get a $150 stipen. uh it has a 57% success rate. Uh we're in 39 cities and that success rate is about double that the regular success rate for online course. Uh so I encourage you if you have people that you think are emerging leaders, I encourage you to get them involved uh with the lived experience training academy. Um, and you know, as I talked about, criminalization has consequences. Uh, I won't go through all those consequences. I think you all know those. Uh, people stay homeless longer. Uh, people have criminal records that keep them from employment, keep them from housing. Uh, people lose connection uh, with the important providers who they've engaged with sometimes over the course of years. Uh so we have to make sure that this is not the solution uh as it is in many cities across the country. We have to make sure we push back on that. So um I'm going to at the end of my remarks today, I will leave some time for questions and answers. Uh but I want to um go into uh my actual speech today. So I want to say uh good morning again. Good morning. All right. Um, and I want to thank the leaders of the Office of Homeless Services. Uh, but not just them. I want to thank the providers, the outreach workers, the housing specialists, the case managers, the elected officials, the advocates, and most importantly, the people with lived experience in this room. Thank you for being here. I'm honored to stand with you in Nashville, a city known around the world for its music. A city built on storytelling, a city where people come chasing dreams. Yet today, many of our neighbors are simply chasing survival. And the reality should challenge every one of us. Because while Nashville continues to grow, while cranes fill the skyline and prosperity reaches new heights, too many of our brothers and sisters are left behind. Today, I want to talk to you about what it means to swim upstream. Because that is exactly what this work feels like. Every day we are swimming against rising housing cost, swimming against shrinking resources, swimming against public misunderstanding, swimming against political attacks, and lately swimming against a growing movement that seeks to criminalize poverty rather than solve it. But I also want to talk to you about why we cannot stop swimming. Because the work represented in this room matters now more than any point in the last decade. When I look at Nashville, I see a city that mirrors what is happening all across America. A city experiencing tremendous economic growth. A city attracting investment. A city becoming increasingly desirable. But I also see a city wrestling with one of the most significant housing affordability challenges in the south. And when housing becomes unaffordable, homelessness rises. Not because people are irresponsible, not because people became suddenly addicted, not because people suddenly became mentally ill, but because housing becomes unaffordable. It's really that simple. Too often, America wants complicated explanations for homelessness. But truth But the truth is awfully is awfully painfully straightforward. When housing costs rise higher than wages, homelessness rises. When affordable housing disappears, homelessness rises. When safety net program shrink, homelessness rises. The latest Nashville homeless data tells a powerful story. In January 2026, nearly 4,000 people were experiencing homelessness in Nashville on a single month snapshot in in January, including hundreds of families and more than 500 children. Over the previous 12 months, more than 12,000 unique people experienced homelessness in this city. The data also reflects participation from 47 service providers working throughout the community. Think about it. 12,000 people, not statistics, people, veterans, families, young adults, seniors, workers, people who once had housing, people who thought homelessness would happen to someone else until it happened to them. And while Nashville's economy continues to grow, thousands of residents remain one crisis away from losing everything. That is not a personal failure. That is a system failure. 40 years ago, America faced a similar reckoning. The modern homelessness crisis emerged into public view during the 1980s. Affordable housing was disappearing. Federal housing investments were shrinking. Economic inequity was widening. And suddenly homelessness became impossible to ignore. People sleeping in train stations, families living in cars, veterans under bridges, encampments and growing in every major city. And from that crisis emerged a movement. Organizations came together, faith communities organized, people with lived experience found their voice, and the National Coalition for the Homeless were born. We were founded on a simple belief. People experiencing homelessness should not merely be served. They should be heard. They should be respected. And they should help lead to solutions. And that belief remains at the heart of our work today. There are moments in social movements when evidence becomes impossible to ignore. Supportive housing created one of those moments. All of these people want to be homeless." So, we went out and we asked and we said, "Hey, do you want to be homeless?" 80% of people said, "That's the dumbest question you have ever asked." But still, that left us with about 20% of people saying, "Yeah, yeah, I do want to be homeless." And so, we went and we we asked some more questions about that. And we said, "Well, what what is it that makes you want to be homeless?" And most of the answers we got were, "Well, you know, I always said I was going to retire to Florida and then I threw my back out and I couldn't work, so I moved down here and now I'm homeless here, so I guess I made it work." Other people said, "You know what? I tried and tried as hard as I possibly could to get out of homelessness and there was nothing I could do about it. So it just feels a little bit better to say this is what I'm trying to do as opposed to say that this is something happening to me." So, we went back and we changed the question and we went and we said, "Hey, okay, listen. Let's ask this a different way. If housing was available to you that was affordable and met your needs, would you still be interested in moving into that housing?" And 96% of people say yes to that question. If housing was available and affordable and met my needs, I would be off the streets in a second. Now, what we are seeing is a lot of unsheltered homelessness grow. And that gets hard because we know what the reality is of the homeless population. We know that the average age of a homeless person in this country is 9 years old. We know that we're seeing more and more families with children become homeless. And we know that most people see only the 30% or so of the the population that's living and experiencing chronic homelessness. Most people just think that that's 100% of the homeless population. And so even as we open up programs, if those folks are still on the street, people start to question what it is we're doing. But the fact that people are on the street has a very clear and direct relationship with the shelter programs that we operate. People may have been rejecting the shelter. May they decided that when they got there, they didn't feel treated like an adult. They didn't feel treated with respect. They weren't offered dignity. They were made to feel less than. Some people get rejected by the shelter and they're told, "Well, if you have a mental health problem or if you don't have an income, then you're not welcome to come in." And when we let shelters operate like that, we create chronic homelessness. That's essentially saying, "Soon as you fixed all your problems, come on in and we'll help you fix all your problems." Imagine if you called the doctor and you're like, "Doctor, I am so sick." And if your doctor said, "I'm so sorry to hear that." As soon as you're not sick anymore, why don't you come by my office and we'll see what we can do? We would think that was a horrible doctor. And yet, we allow shelters to operate in the same way so that there is a mismatch between the services that they are offering and what people on the street actually need. Now, I want to take on just a couple common myths around what we see in the community and what we see in the population. And these are the points of push back that we always get. First, of course, there is this great rumor that nobody ever lived here homeless before homeless services showed up. There's a story somewhere being told right now that the only reason there's people homeless in Nashville is because some shelter serves hot dogs on Tuesday night. And people were taking buses from across the country to come in here and and get those free hot dogs. In most communities, about 75% of the homeless population is homegrown. People who lived and worked before becoming homeless in that community. And for the remainder, about half are from elsewhere in the state. And yeah, there is some movement. And that's mostly people doing everything they can to meet their needs, just as you would do if your family was in crisis. We often hear that people need treatment before they can be successfully housed. According to the substance use, substance abuse and mental health services administration, there's about a million people in Tennessee who meet the DSM5 criteria for a substance use disorder. Proportionally, that would translate to roughly 100,000 people in Nashville on any given night who meet the definition of having a substance use disorder. And yet only 2,000 people are homeless tonight. Which tells us that for 98% of people in this community, maybe sobriety isn't a precondition to get into housing. And in fact, people can be housed and and retain and regrow and and come back to the place where they had been before simply by having that safety and that security of housing. We often hear that people living in encampments don't want housing. And the reality of it is again 96% of people do. They just don't know where to go to get it. And when they do get it, sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn't. I heard Dr. Cho reference this earlier. We act as if everybody on the street should be ready to change at any given moment. that in fact when I as an outreach worker show up with a clipboard and a lanyard that the the right response is somebody's going to say, "Oh, thank goodness you're here. I've been waiting." And the reality is most people are so caught up just trying to survive that it's been real hard for them to even thinking to even start thinking about change. So folks who are living in encampments aren't living there because they've decided between that and a one-bedroom and a studio apartment. They're there because camps provide some degree of safety and some degree of holding on to who you were as all of the rest of your identity starts to slip away after living without housing for a while. And of course, we always hear despite the fact that every control group study has shown housing to be the most effective intervention we can have that housing focused responses to homelessness do not work. The reality of it is, if you want to help people achieve sobriety, house them first. If you want to help people improve their mental health, house them first. If you want to help people improve their social relations, their connections with their friends, with their family, house them first. If we want people to get back to work, we've got to house them first. So what we know is we've got about 19,000 people becoming homeless in our country every week. 19,000. That's the inflow. That's what we are up against just to keep things the same. System-wise, for every person who becomes homeless, there's only one shelter bed for every three people who are out there. And not all of those shelters are actually getting to serve the people who truly need the most help. So even with only one out of every three people being able to access a shelter bed, then we of course have shelters that are broken down by subopuls. This one's only for youth. This one's only for families. This one's only for people who don't have any problems or have many, many fewer problems than so many other shelters are trying to serve. These are the shelters that will tell us, well, you know, we have a 95% success rate, but will fail to say that 80% of the people who truly needed help weren't able to get into those programs to begin with. So, we have these needs and these opportunities to realign the services that we do have because odds are we're not going to see a whole lot more money in the next couple of years. So, we've got to make sure that what we're doing is as effective as possible. And that's on the technical side, but we also have to make sure that our services are as human as possible. On the relational side, we often talk about readiness as if it was somebody being ready to move into housing because that's what they've decided they want or not. But readiness is so much more often a state of somebody's nervous system about whether they feel safe, whether they feel that they can trust the provider who they're working with, whether it ultimately makes sense to put all of that effort into getting people into housing. We know the world of substances has changed. Most of our treatment models today are based around the idea that everybody uses one substance of choice. And in reality, we are now in a poly substance crisis. Heck, I' I've been around in this work for 30 years, have been through the crack cocaine epidemic, have been through the alcohol epidemic. I have heard people in our industry say, "You know what would be amazing? Let's bring back crack because somehow that was easier than serving people on methamphetamine and fentanyl. Somehow more predictable. Somehow we still knew what to do. But we have to catch up on what the realities are and what's happening in our communities. And finally, we have to acknowledge that there's some real trauma for people who are out on the street. Not just from the experiences they may have had as a child, not just from the experiences they may have had sliding into homelessness, but the experience of homelessness in and of itself is traumatic. People are trying to get their needs met on a daily basis and all of this has a huge impact. Trauma changes everything. It changes how people feel about them themselves, about other people, about what safety is if good things happen to them. In short, trauma can change your perspective of the world from I think the world is a pretty good place where every once in a while a bad thing happens to suddenly the whole world is scary and frightening and every once in a while something good happens. And if we're not adapting our services to actually show up and treat people in a way that recognizes the prevalence of trauma in the community, we are missing an opportunity to connect with them in a very real way. So at the end of the day, despite the current cultural narrative around this, homelessness is not a punishment. Homelessness is not a sign of character failure, of character flaws. It is the inevitable outcome of housing unaffordability. And what we have going on with housing right now is not sustainable. And if homelessness is not a punishment, then we should be able to agree that housing is not a reward. Housing is a basic human right as much as food or water. And heck, we end up having these kind these fights in our communities all the time where people do not want to see another human being living and dying on the street. And they also don't want to see new affordable housing going up in their community. And you can't have it both ways. You can be against new affordable housing or you can be against seeing other human beings living and dying on the street. But you can't be against both because one is the solution to the other. Now, when working with people, we have a lot of different ways we can break them into subpopuls into different typologies. newly homeless, long-term homeless, chronic homeless, domestic violence, children, youth, veterans, anything like that. But I found the most helpful way of understanding what people have going on right now is this. People are on one of two paths when they're living outside or in shelters. Generally, people start on the first path and that is becoming homeless and doing everything in their power that they can do to escape homelessness as quickly as possible. And when that fails, they start the other path, which is doing everything in their power to help people survive, to help themselves survive, to endure being homeless. And being in that survival state is a psychological adaptation and that's going to affect what people are doing. I mean, heck, we show up and we're like, "We made an appointment for you in six weeks. Good news." And they're like, "The only time that exists right now is today and tonight because I'm just trying to survive." So, there's even a mismatch there. And we have to get to that really relational part of what we're trying to do if we're ever going to get there. and and that really lives and dies with our own emotional intelligence. We talk a lot about the core service orientation and I will say as this as the federal funding landscape continues to change it is more important than ever that we come back to these that we are trauma informed that we recognize the prevalence of trauma and that we adapt our services to actually minimize any additional harm we might do to people. We have to reduce harms and we have to promote wellness. We have to understand that sometimes we have to meet people's immediate needs before we can start even talking about long-term goals. We've got to be non-judgmental, staying in that place of curiosity rather than of judgment. To quote the great father Greg Bole from Homeboy Industries, "We stand in awe of what the people we serve carry, not in judgment of how they hold it. We are motivational instead of demanding supporting people to make transformational changes in their lives but not demanding it. We stay focused on recovery. Recovery being all of that space between homeless and housed, using and not using, mentally ill and well, and understand that there is a gradient. There is an incremental improvement that people can make in their lives even in the presence of symptoms that may still exist. And we stay strength-based and person- centered, meaning that we see what people are capable of doing. We understand that most of the people we serve have survived things that would kill most of us. That people have strengths of survival, of service navigation. And with all of this, it only works with our own emotional intelligence. That is our secret weapon as workers in this. Because when we show up with emotional intelligence, when we show up emotionally grounded, when we are so calm in an interaction that somebody can borrow our calm, that's when people start to get emotionally regulated and be able to make decisions. You ever notice that when you get stressed, your ability to make really thoughtful, good, wellthoughtout decisions kinds of goes away? Well, carry that over to survival mode and it has the same effect on people. So, we do have to make sure we're regulated. We have to stay curious. We have to listen to what people tell us what they need. We've got to be kind and clear and direct. If I had any one thing I try to carry across the country, it is this. People living without housing can go anywhere to be treated poorly. They can go anywhere to feel unseen and unheard and disrespected and invisible. So they damn well ne better not be coming to our programs to feel that way. We have an opportunity to create these connections with folks. And from that first connection, that's where the quality relationship that's needed for transformational change starts. We separate the person from the problem. We understand that people have problems, sure, but the housing crisis is the problem. The person is not the problem. And we focus on what we can control. very often right now that is just our response. How we show up and how we take care of ourselves so that we can be in this work for a long time because we very often say things or hear things like, "Oh, they're burning out. Maybe they're not cut out for this work. Oh, they've they've absorbed too much vicarious trauma. They're having a strong emotional reaction to the fact that somebody is suffering right in front of them. Maybe they're not cut out for this work." And it's time we start acknowledging that things like burnout and moral injury and vicarious trauma are not shortcomings. They are occupational hazards in this work as much as in any other industry where there are things that can affect people over the years as they do the work. And so we have to be a be able to take care of ourselves and be able to take care of each other in order to do that. Now, I want to close with just a quick look at how people change because we have some funny ideas about how people should change when we show up and we're like, "Hey, here's an opportunity." Most people think change looks a little bit like this. We go over, we flip on the light switch, and change happens. I would ask first, has anybody in here or any of you rocking a 100% success rate in trying to improve your lives? Anybody like exactly where you want to be? No. I mean, for me, even when I do want to change, I'm probably going to call a therapist. I'm probably going to call make an appointment in what is that called? A therapeutic environment. I'm going to show up sober. I have my own transportation. I know what I want to talk about. I'm excited to talk about this. and I still get it right like 30% of the time. And yet we ask people who are living and dying on the street, not sure where they're going to eat tonight, where they're going to put their stuff, where they're going to go to the bathroom, how they're going to feel safe to be fully prepared to change at any given moment. Most change looks a lot more like this. There's this big messy middle right in there that is all kinds of ups and downs and reconsideration and ambivalence and all this stuff. And we're probably familiar with the stages of change. And I'll go through this just very very briefly. Pre-contemplation kind of helps us understand well somebody's not quite there, not thinking about change. Somebody's contemplating change that means they're thinking about doing something different in the next six months. From there they move into preparing to do something in the next 30 days. Then they're taking action. Then they're maintaining it. From there, they either keep maintaining that change or maybe there's a relapse. First of all, that relapse is not a failure. That relapse is direct evidence that you are involved in a change process. And I tell you that as somebody in recovery myself, who did not get clean the first time 14, 15 years ago or the second or the third, fourth, fifth, or sixth time. And if anybody had just said, "You're not trying hard enough." At any point in those first six attempts, it would have undermined every bit of confidence, every bit of readiness, every bit of importance that had. We have to understand that the change process can take some time even when it's held up against the realities of yeah, human change takes a while. Take as much time as you need as long as it's in 30 days or less. We have to understand that there is again sometimes a mismatch between these things. And the thing I want you to take away from this based on studies of people in crisis thinking about change, 40% of people in crisis are in the pre-contemplation stage at any given time. Another 40% are in the contemplation stage. That means only one out of five people in crisis is preparing to change, making action steps to change, maintaining a change, or doing any of those other things. And yet we believe that 100% of people should be ready. And all of the data says it would actually be really weird if somebody walked up and were like, "Hey, what do you think about housing?" And they were like, "Thank god you're here." In fact, the odds are that we're going to have to work with them to move through that. And that's going to take time and that's going to take human connection. I will close with this. At the end of the day, the work that we're doing comes down to this question. What problem are we actually trying to solve? Because if we think the problem is that people don't have enough food and don't have enough cups of coffee and don't have enough socks, well then we might measure our success by counting how much food we give out and how much coffee we give out and how many socks we give out. If we think that the problem is that people don't have the life skills that they need to survive, then we might measure success by how many programs we can put people through. But if we think that the problem is that people don't have a safe and affordable place to call home, then the only way for us to measure success is by how many people we've moved into housing and how quickly we are able to do that. This calls on us to do a couple different things. One, we have to make sure that all of our programs are actually oriented toward housing, that they're actually trying to solve the actual problem that folks have. We need to make sure our shelters have the lowest barriers possible so that the people who actually need that help can get that help. And we need to make sure that we don't give up in this work. If there's anything that has kept me going, especially through the pandemic, through all of this work that we have done, it's the words of Shane Quigan, and to paraphrase his great poem, our sweat will always have more value than our tears. The work that we do today is going to make an enormous impact for one life and then to continue to demonstrate that how we are doing this works. But through all of it, we have to be working with absolute certainty that housing is the only thing that's going to solve this. If we have people who don't have a home, getting them into a home solves that problem. If we have communities that are tired, like us, of seeing other human beings living and dying on the street, well, helping people move into housing and start rebuilding their lives solves that problem. And if we're working to improve our communities in any other way, [snorts] we understand that access to that safe and affordable place to call home is what everything else is driven from, what everything else relies on so that people can actually live their lives and be part of their communities once more. Thank you so much. [applause] Um uh the first question is given its measurable success, why are so many people so deeply opposed to h the housing first model and what are primary contributing factors? I don't have a good answer for why other than people have been led to believe that even though their rent went up to $1,800, 2,200, $2,400 a month. And even though there's six empty apartments on either side of where they're living, that the problem is that we're giving free hot dogs to people who are living out on the street or that we are solving the problem of homelessness by actually moving people into an apartment and then working with them to reconnect and get jobs and do all of these different things. So in terms of how this this narrative around housing first being the enemy has really come to be, it starts with well orchestrated PR campaigns against it. It starts with and and I don't know maybe this is a coincidence starts with the fact that the people telling us that housing first isn't working are the same people who own the jails and the prisons that they're trying to put people in instead of housing. Coincidence probably, right? >> Many of our clients would prefer to be on the streets rather than in shelters due to how they are treated in shelters. What can we do to improve the services we offer in shelters? So this is a great example of where emotional intelligence comes into this because we can train people all with all of the technical detail in the world on what it means to be trauma informed on what it means to be motivational. But if at some point we're not able to show up as an ally, which would mean calm, which would mean able to listen, which would mean not judging people for what they're sharing with us. If we were able to show up that way, we would be able to carry out those core competencies of of everything from crisis deescalation to motivational interviewing to case management 101 starts with the quality of the relationship we have. And so sometimes we do end up with people who are really insistent on carrying this old outdated disproven model of shelter forward that does leave people feeling mistreated. That does leave people feeling disrespected. I will never forget a time when I was at a shelter watching a 20-year-old staff member tell a 65year-old man it was time for him to go to bed. Like there's all of these different things that we have that ultimately create barriers to whether people are comfortable coming into programs. And if those barriers end up leaving people feeling less safe or less respected or less dignified than they might stay out on the street, that's a rational decision that somebody might make. So I think in that to that question, the answer doesn't lie in how do we get the people on the street to think differently about the shelters. It's how do we get the shelters to show up differently for the people who truly need those services? >> Awesome. [applause] Where do communities typically get the homelessness response system wrong? And part two to that, in your 30 years of experience, what interventions or policies have you seen to be most effective with getting it right? >> Where we get it wrong most often is a mismatch between why homelessness is happening and the realities of the job market and the housing market. We and there are good reasons that we all think that homelessness is a matter of personal failure. In the early 80s when homelessness first exploded on the national scene, we had people seeing folks and I was growing up in New York at the time. So just seeing human beings living and dying on the street was just about the most normal thing in the world. That's why I do this work because I won't let my kids growing up grow up to think that this is normal. But when that first happened, we had people walking around saying, "Huh gosh, I thought this was the land of opportunity. I thought this was the greatest nation on earth. I thought anybody could be anything they wanted to become." created this sense of cognitive dissonance. And so when the government initially funded homeless services, they did not fund housing solutions. They did not fund structural anti-poverty solutions. No, they said, "Here's how we solve homelessness. Substance abuse and mental health." SAMA, the two individual factors for this entire structural, societal, systemic problem. And we decided that the solution was to fix the people rather than to fix the system. And I think to some extent many of us bought into that and that is carried into how we are getting it wrong. That we understand that for the most part if we're going to have uh a generous interpretation or in fact just hold people in unconditional positive regard we've got to understand people are generally doing the best they can possibly do with the information and the knowledges and the resources they have available. Second part of that, what solutions work? Not to sound like a broken record, but housing. This is wild, right? People don't have a house, they need a house, they get a house. Problem solved. Does it solve every problem? No, absolutely not. In fact, we barely have enough money to end half of homelessness. So, we can't jump into also trying to solve poverty and also trying to solve all these other things. We've got to count on that there's other awesome people doing the same work in those fields as we are doing here. But at the end of the day, nothing has been as successful as simply moving people into housing. And we've had great opportunities to demonstrate that that is absolutely true. First, when the VA funded early trials of housing first and we saw suddenly veterans became the fastest decreasing subpopul of homelessness during the pandemic. terrible, terrible time. But for some of us, we were like, "Wow, we might actually get the money that we need to solve this problem." And I saw shelters that were going from housing 200 people a year to housing 600 people a year just because we moved people in quickly. And I'll say the final piece of that is looking at shallow subsidies. The reality is if we've moved people into permanent supportive housing, after a couple years, many of them don't need that ongoing intensive support. They've stabilized. They've done exactly what the housing was intended to do and yet they stay there because they still can't afford to move someplace else. So, we've got people in permanent supportive housing units for $20,000 a year. But gosh, if we took a family of four who just couldn't afford the last $400 of their rent, well, if we just put $400 a month toward their rent, kept that family housed, then we keep four people housed for $4,800 a year. So there are so many different ways that we have yet to fully and and intentionally explore what some additional support might look like and there's so many opportunities to do that. >> Awesome. And whoever wrote this question, I appreciate it. As a messenger, how do we and definitely this was our attempt today. How do we strike that balance between informing others like our community and our council members and everyone who helps us makes decisions about this work? How do we strike the balance of [clears throat] not catastrophizing, if I could say, and I'm going to put that in quotes because that's what's on here. catastrophizing the numbers and also not being overly optimistic about the numbers. Where is that balance? I'm going to pull first from a rule of thumb from fundraising. And when we were doing a lot of fundraising for my shelter, the general approach was to understand that 20% of people are going to love what we're doing no matter what because they know it's the right thing to do. It aligns with their values. It aligns with the core of their identity. 20% of people are going to hate what we do no matter what. I don't know why. I can't figure it out, but it's there. And they tend to be the loudest. and they tend to be the ones we want to respond to. But there's 60% of the people in the middle who maybe haven't made up their mind too much in one direction or another and are willing to consider the arguments of the other side. And I think that's where we focus our attention, not in the people who are so entrenched in just anger and hate and grievance that there's nothing we could say to satisfy them, but to talk to the folks who are actually willing to have conversations. And I will tell you, I used to get asked to go speak about homelessness at the shelter and I'd be brought into a business and they'd say, "Hey, listen. We're glad you're here to talk about homelessness, but the reason that we actually brought you here is there's this guy who's sleeping on our doorway and we don't know what to do." 10 years later, those same businesses were bringing me back and they were saying, "Hey, listen. We're so glad that you're here. But listen, why we really brought you in is our administrative assistant just had to move out of town because she can't afford to live in this community anymore. And now she's driving 40 miles each way to work. And one of my junior engineers, he also had to move out of town because he can't afford to live here. And I say that to just surface this understanding that homelessness is getting closer to home for more people than I think are able to admit it right now. And so right now that's where we see the ferocity of these anti-housing first campaigns because it's becoming more real and more viscerable more visceral for more people. So that's why we're [snorts] seeing more and more of this fight against what the right thing to do is. So all we need to do is keep going. Keep having honest conversations, but also if you come across somebody who you're crystal clear there's just nothing you can do to change their mind. Move on and try for the next person. >> All right, let's give the Carmine a hand. >> Thanks. >> All right, everybody. [applause] Good job. We're going to take a brief break right here. I know it says 12:05. You're going to have 10 minutes. So, if you could come back at 12:10, that would be perfect. I'm sure you're going to want to hear from director of office of homeless services, the overview, and you all know her, Allison Kentwe. Really good information coming up. This has been a service of the Metro Nashville Network. If you would like to see this presentation again or for more information on this and other programs, visit nashville.gov.

I think you all have already found the restrooms, but if you haven't already, there are both men and women's restrooms located to the back of the room, the right and left of you. So, welcome, welcome everyone to the 2026 State of Homelessness Symposium. Many of you know me, but I'm going to introduce myself anyway. I am Demetrius Cheney. I'm the public information officer for the office of homeless services. It is an honor to have you in the room again this year. Raise your hand if you were here last year. Great, great, great. Raise your hand if you are new to the symposium experience. Well, welcome. Welcome. You picked a great year to be here. Um before we begin, I want to thank many leaders, partners, advocates, uh the mayor's office, Metro Council, our homelessness planning um council and chair, uh the continuum of care, the office of homeless services staff, service providers, community organizations, funders, advocates, and friends who have joined us today. Thank you so much for being here. Thank you for your partnership, your leadership, and your continued commitment to our neighbors experiencing homelessness. Before we begin, I want to acknowledge something that many of us have probably already thought about. If you um are here for the first time or if you are returning, why is this symposium like um a celebration of sorts when there are still so many people homeless? You may be wondering that and that is a very valid question. Here's the answer. We don't wait until every challenge is solved before we start recognizing the lives that have already been impacted by change. We don't wait until every funding stream ends before celebrating the partnerships that have already transformed our community. We don't wait until the work is finished to acknowledge the people like yourselves who've poured their time, expertise, and compassion into moving this work forward. Another thought, some of you may also be thinking, "The numbers in this report are static. In fact, they are already changing." You are exactly right. Since this report was printed, more people have been housed through flexible funding and housing programs. And you are also correct. More people have become homeless. This work continues. That reality feels uncomfortable, which is why we're here today. We want a clear finish line. And the truth is that every finish line in this work often becomes the starting point for the next challenge. How many of you agree with that? Yeah. Every person housed creates an opportunity to focus on the next person still waiting. Every success reveals where more work remains. And today you're going to hear about lots of successes. But what you'll also hear is there is so much opportunity for more to be done. So yes, today is about celebration, but more importantly, today is about holding that tension between homelessness and housing and working together as a com as a community to close the distance between the two. I will say that again. today is about holding that tension between homelessness and housing and working together as a community to close the distance between them. Thank you all for being here. We look forward to the work that we're going to do in this next and I will say in this next six months but also in this next year. So let's begin. Our first keynote speaker, Donald Whitehead Jr. is a nationally recognized advocate, policy leader, and person in long-term recovery.
