And that's going to take time and that's going to take human connection. I will close with this. At the end of the day, the work that we're doing comes down to this question. What problem are we actually trying to solve? Because if we think the problem is that people don't have enough food and don't have enough cups of coffee and don't have enough socks, well then we might measure our success by counting how much food we give out and how much coffee we give out and how many socks we give out. If we think that the problem is that people don't have the life skills that they need to survive, then we might measure success by how many programs we can put people through. But if we think that the problem is that people don't have a safe and affordable place to call home, then the only way for us to measure success is by how many people we've moved into housing and how quickly we are able to do that. This calls on us to do a couple different things. One, we have to make sure that all of our programs are actually oriented toward housing, that they're actually trying to solve the actual problem that folks have. We need to make sure our shelters have the lowest barriers possible so that the people who actually need that help can get that help. And we need to make sure that we don't give up in this work. If there's anything that has kept me going, especially through the pandemic, through all of this work that we have done, it's the words of Shane Quigan, and to paraphrase his great poem, our sweat will always have more value than our tears. The work that we do today is going to make an enormous impact for one life and then to continue to demonstrate that how we are doing this works. But through all of it, we have to be working with absolute certainty that housing is the only thing that's going to solve this. If we have people who don't have a home, getting them into a home solves that problem. If we have communities that are tired, like us, of seeing other human beings living and dying on the street, well, helping people move into housing and start rebuilding their lives solves that problem. And if we're working to improve our communities in any other way, [snorts] we understand that access to that safe and affordable place to call home is what everything else is driven from, what everything else relies on so that people can actually live their lives and be part of their communities once more. Thank you so much. [applause] Um uh the first question is given its measurable success, why are so many people so deeply opposed to h the housing first model and what are primary contributing factors? I don't have a good answer for why other than people have been led to believe that even though their rent went up to $1,800, 2,200, $2,400 a month. And even though there's six empty apartments on either side of where they're living, that the problem is that we're giving free hot dogs to people who are living out on the street or that we are solving the problem of homelessness by actually moving people into an apartment and then working with them to reconnect and get jobs and do all of these different things. So in terms of how this this narrative around housing first being the enemy has really come to be, it starts with well orchestrated PR campaigns against it. It starts with and and I don't know maybe this is a coincidence starts with the fact that the people telling us that housing first isn't working are the same people who own the jails and the prisons that they're trying to put people in instead of housing. Coincidence probably, right? >> Many of our clients would prefer to be on the streets rather than in shelters due to how they are treated in shelters. What can we do to improve the services we offer in shelters? So this is a great example of where emotional intelligence comes into this because we can train people all with all of the technical detail in the world on what it means to be trauma informed on what it means to be motivational. But if at some point we're not able to show up as an ally, which would mean calm, which would mean able to listen, which would mean not judging people for what they're sharing with us. If we were able to show up that way, we would be able to carry out those core competencies of of everything from crisis deescalation to motivational interviewing to case management 101 starts with the quality of the relationship we have. And so sometimes we do end up with people who are really insistent on carrying this old outdated disproven model of shelter forward that does leave people feeling mistreated. That does leave people feeling disrespected. I will never forget a time when I was at a shelter watching a 20-year-old staff member tell a 65year-old man it was time for him to go to bed. Like there's all of these different things that we have that ultimately create barriers to whether people are comfortable coming into programs. And if those barriers end up leaving people feeling less safe or less respected or less dignified than they might stay out on the street, that's a rational decision that somebody might make. So I think in that to that question, the answer doesn't lie in how do we get the people on the street to think differently about the shelters. It's how do we get the shelters to show up differently for the people who truly need those services? >> Awesome. [applause] Where do communities typically get the homelessness response system wrong? And part two to that, in your 30 years of experience, what interventions or policies have you seen to be most effective with getting it right? >> Where we get it wrong most often is a mismatch between why homelessness is happening and the realities of the job market and the housing market. We and there are good reasons that we all think that homelessness is a matter of personal failure. In the early 80s when homelessness first exploded on the national scene, we had people seeing folks and I was growing up in New York at the time. So just seeing human beings living and dying on the street was just about the most normal thing in the world. That's why I do this work because I won't let my kids growing up grow up to think that this is normal. But when that first happened, we had people walking around saying, "Huh gosh, I thought this was the land of opportunity. I thought this was the greatest nation on earth. I thought anybody could be anything they wanted to become." created this sense of cognitive dissonance. And so when the government initially funded homeless services, they did not fund housing solutions. They did not fund structural anti-poverty solutions. No, they said, "Here's how we solve homelessness. Substance abuse and mental health." SAMA, the two individual factors for this entire structural, societal, systemic problem. And we decided that the solution was to fix the people rather than to fix the system. And I think to some extent many of us bought into that and that is carried into how we are getting it wrong. That we understand that for the most part if we're going to have uh a generous interpretation or in fact just hold people in unconditional positive regard we've got to understand people are generally doing the best they can possibly do with the information and the knowledges and the resources they have available. Second part of that, what solutions work? Not to sound like a broken record, but housing. This is wild, right? People don't have a house, they need a house, they get a house. Problem solved. Does it solve every problem? No, absolutely not. In fact, we barely have enough money to end half of homelessness. So, we can't jump into also trying to solve poverty and also trying to solve all these other things. We've got to count on that there's other awesome people doing the same work in those fields as we are doing here. But at the end of the day, nothing has been as successful as simply moving people into housing. And we've had great opportunities to demonstrate that that is absolutely true. First, when the VA funded early trials of housing first and we saw suddenly veterans became the fastest decreasing subpopul of homelessness during the pandemic. terrible, terrible time. But for some of us, we were like, "Wow, we might actually get the money that we need to solve this problem." And I saw shelters that were going from housing 200 people a year to housing 600 people a year just because we moved people in quickly. And I'll say the final piece of that is looking at shallow subsidies. The reality is if we've moved people into permanent supportive housing, after a couple years, many of them don't need that ongoing intensive support. They've stabilized. They've done exactly what the housing was intended to do and yet they stay there because they still can't afford to move someplace else. So, we've got people in permanent supportive housing units for $20,000 a year. But gosh, if we took a family of four who just couldn't afford the last $400 of their rent, well, if we just put $400 a month toward their rent, kept that family housed, then we keep four people housed for $4,800 a year. So there are so many different ways that we have yet to fully and and intentionally explore what some additional support might look like and there's so many opportunities to do that. >> Awesome. And whoever wrote this question, I appreciate it. As a messenger, how do we and definitely this was our attempt today. How do we strike that balance between informing others like our community and our council members and everyone who helps us makes decisions about this work? How do we strike the balance of [clears throat] not catastrophizing, if I could say, and I'm going to put that in quotes because that's what's on here. catastrophizing the numbers and also not being overly optimistic about the numbers. Where is that balance? I'm going to pull first from a rule of thumb from fundraising. And when we were doing a lot of fundraising for my shelter, the general approach was to understand that 20% of people are going to love what we're doing no matter what because they know it's the right thing to do. It aligns with their values. It aligns with the core of their identity. 20% of people are going to hate what we do no matter what. I don't know why. I can't figure it out, but it's there. And they tend to be the loudest. and they tend to be the ones we want to respond to. But there's 60% of the people in the middle who maybe haven't made up their mind too much in one direction or another and are willing to consider the arguments of the other side. And I think that's where we focus our attention, not in the people who are so entrenched in just anger and hate and grievance that there's nothing we could say to satisfy them, but to talk to the folks who are actually willing to have conversations. And I will tell you, I used to get asked to go speak about homelessness at the shelter and I'd be brought into a business and they'd say, "Hey, listen. We're glad you're here to talk about homelessness, but the reason that we actually brought you here is there's this guy who's sleeping on our doorway and we don't know what to do." 10 years later, those same businesses were bringing me back and they were saying, "Hey, listen. We're so glad that you're here. But listen, why we really brought you in is our administrative assistant just had to move out of town because she can't afford to live in this community anymore. And now she's driving 40 miles each way to work. And one of my junior engineers, he also had to move out of town because he can't afford to live here. And I say that to just surface this understanding that homelessness is getting closer to home for more people than I think are able to admit it right now. And so right now that's where we see the ferocity of these anti-housing first campaigns because it's becoming more real and more viscerable more visceral for more people. So that's why we're [snorts] seeing more and more of this fight against what the right thing to do is. So all we need to do is keep going. Keep having honest conversations, but also if you come across somebody who you're crystal clear there's just nothing you can do to change their mind. Move on and try for the next person. >> All right, let's give the Carmine a hand. >> Thanks. >> All right, everybody. [applause] Good job. We're going to take a brief break right here. I know it says 12:05. You're going to have 10 minutes. So, if you could come back at 12:10, that would be perfect. I'm sure you're going to want to hear from director of office of homeless services, the overview, and you all know her, Allison Kentwe. Really good information coming up. This has been a service of the Metro Nashville Network. If you would like to see this presentation again or for more information on this and other programs, visit nashville.gov.

Um I would just I would just encourage you if if there are opportunities in departments and maybe you could just send maybe you already send something to departments but like this training is a good example to me like opportunities for you to appear before some of these departments and say to them hey this is the avenue by which you know you need to let your employees know that they can report fraud waste and abuse we will investigate it. We'll do that because I think that there's probably more. >> Yes. >> Out there that we can. >> Yes. And so with that 18, that's actually higher than it was last year. But since then, um, since, well, since Paul started, um, we've created an online training. It's required training or it's sent out. It's not required. New hires all get it. Everybody at Metro whenever you start, there are certain required trainings such as your IT trainings and sexual harassment. Um, and they're automatically assigned. HR is automatically assigning it technically is optional. So we have the new hires. Um we are working with the mayor's office to determine the best avenue as far as getting executive order or is it council legislation because there's such a variety of oversight I guess and how to make something required within Metro determining whether or not it's an executive order. Kind of like our some of our other trainings like um diversity and sexual harassment training. Those are executive order. they do not hit every department because of certain pieces within Metro and its complexities. Um, but we're exploring that avenue to make sure that then we can have it required annually so they're at least getting the annual touch point. Um there's other things that we've thought about newsletters and um presentations to departments, but to your point, if there are presentations, we can reach out and start to try and make those connections um to find other avenues to jump in and kind of layer on to what it's already being done within departments. >> Great. >> And so from a training standpoint, you mean about fraud, waste, and abuse and the function of internal audit just so at the at the onboarding stage. It's a nice little 15inute video. Um, it doesn't have like a quiz or there's questions within it. It's not like quiz format. Um, but we developed it with its soc. Um, and at the end of it, it does like it goes through what is fraud, waste, and abuse. Um, it also covers how do you report it and it also covers the fact that there is a requirement there's one you can always report to the state as well. Um, and that there's also a requirement within 5 days to report likely fraud to the state. I really appreciate um you doing that and I do think whether by executive order or otherwise because um we started this year for the first time. I had Lauren and the team come to present to the metro council orientation because I will tell you when I was a council member by pure happen stance when I was doing my state required we are a waterboard training where you had a whole menu and you could kind of click click click and you had to do let's just say maybe you had to do 15 of 20 pre-recorded whatever of course I clicked the fraud waste and abuse one but I didn't have to right and I realize particular to that earlier matter we were discussing when I felt that that was not appropriately or as robustly addressed knowing what I know now I should have taken that to the state I mean it did rise to that level but I on my honor didn't know that I thought I had fulfilled my duty to report by taking it to the then auditor and so I do think that's an important kind of baseline awareness for all employees and all elected officials. Yes. >> Yeah. We do cover the responsibility because anybody who works for Metro government has a duty to report. >> Y >> next we have our budget. We're under budget right now. It's because consulting invoices hasn't come through yet. Um but we're working our way through. It's also part two. >> We love to hear it. >> I know. >> We love to hear folks under budget. Well, it's also because we have currently have one vacancy um which goes into the next the audit staffing. Um as Bill mentioned, we had Kaylee Harris who left us to go to law school. Um she was our investigator too. But in the meantime, we have actually hired two new auditor ones. We have hired Annayia Grant and Utang um who are now our auditor ones. and we lucked into the fact that one of our other recently hired auditor ones who has been helping Paul in Kayle's absence um he has a passion for for investigations. So, and it takes a special person to do investigations um to to want to do them. Um they're not always fun. >> And so we are in the process of exploring potentially moving him over into the investigative side. We had a really great audit auditor one pull. So, in the event that that move happens, um, we will likely be able to pull from that >> if we if that person still wants to. >> That's good to hear. >> Um, so that's kind of all the shifts around for us. And that's all we have for them. >> Any considerations for future meetings we need to put out there? All right. Uh, then I declare the public meeting adjourned.

docs.text: The meeting is now called to order. We have public comments. Yes. We had a public comment sign-up sheet per the audit committee standards that were set when this was established. We will listen to a maximum of eight people for two minutes each. Mr. Walker will time each individual. He will call each person out and will give a 30-second warning whenever you're close to the time and then once the timer goes off, that is the end of the two-minute period. Okay, first person we have is Tim Lee. Good evening. I'm here to talk about the audit with the Office of Homeless Services. I guess you've got two audits that you're considering. I've worked with the COC, which is not under your prurory, but I've seen nothing but professionalism from the Office of Homeless Services. And I've looked over the letter that Ms. Welch has submitted with all the complaints. I just find it a little bit over the top, and I think it's more of a packed job. And I have all the confidence in the world of the Office of Homeless Services. There's a real backbone behind getting a homeless situation under control. The COC is not helping a whole lot. And I would like you to kind of consider not doing an audit on any of these complaints that have been issued by Ms. Welch. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. All right. The next person is Mr. Derrick McCloud. Hello, everyone. My name is Derrick McCloud, and I'm very grateful for the Office of Homeless Services. I am a resident at Strobel House. Due to being homeless and living a very destructive life, the Office of Homeless Services has given me an opportunity to have a place to call home. That place to call home has allowed me to get enrolled at Nashville State Community College, where I am majoring in social work and about to be inducted into the Phi Beta Kappa National Honor Society. This January also has allowed me to get licensed in ministry, all because I've had a place to call home. So, please, let's do the right thing about the Office of Homeless Services. Thank you. Thank you. All right. Mark Chandler. My name is Mark Chandler, and I'm a resident of Roadway, Harding Place. Office of Homeless Services pretty much saved my life. I was living in Tent City, and they closed Tent City down. When I first got there, I didn't want to be there. I thought it was like jail. But since then, I have a new view of how I've been in that place out there. It's allowed me to, like you said, I can call home. And by extension, the people that run it out there, the hospitality hub, they're not like any other agency I've dealt with. You're not a statistic out there. These people really care about you. You know, whatever you need, they're there. You know, if I need someone to talk to, they're there. You know, if I need a bus pass, if I need to get my ID, whatever I need to get to get to permanent housing. Not just get permanent housing, but have a foundation under me that supports sustainability. That I can, you know, when I leave there, I can maintain that. They're there, you know. I think it's the best thing that ever happened to homelessness in Nashville. And I've been around homelessness. I've been homeless on and off for 20 years. You know, I've dealt with Salvation Army, Rumanian. There's nothing like OHS. It's the best thing that ever happened to be seated in terms of homelessness. Thank you. Thank you. Allyson Cantway. Hi, my name is Allison Cantway. I'm the Assistant Director of Planning and Research at the Office of Homeless Services. I just want to start by saying that OHS has nothing to hide. We're really proud of the work that we're doing. We share more data with the community than nearly any department we share. This 20-slide deck with literally hundreds of numbers once a month at the Public Health and Safety Committee. And we do this because it's important for us to be good stewards of public funding. And we've committed to being open and transparent. We're not perfect, but we've made corrections along the way. We're always open to hearing about ways that we can improve. But we've been under investigations, audits, and ethical complaints, many of them that have originated from a single council member, which have not found major issues with our department. We're currently under an internal investigation that was initiated by the same person. To address largely the same inaccurate allegations. You know, I've been with OHS since it was created in 2023. I spent about five years previously in another metro department that did similar work, similar size. In my time there, we were just never targeted like this. And all of this takes precious staff time away from serving the most vulnerable among us, which is why we all joined this department. Our office has been committed to serving the most vulnerable population that is least likely to access services. I know there are people in the community that don't agree with us serving this population, but these people want and they deserve a bed, air conditioning, a shower, a door to close, and a place to live safely. This is not easy. Providing housing to those that need it most can be really hard. And unfortunately, just like in apartment complexes and subdivisions, there can be emphasis of theft, violence, fires, arguments. These challenges are not unique to Nashville and happen in all residential facilities, unfortunately. But our Housing First and Trauma Informed principles tell us that we must continue no matter how hard the work is. I'm proud of the work that we've done. I think that Nashville should be proud of the work that we've done. And while we absolutely want to be transparent and provide accountability, we care most about making sure that all Nashvillians are able to secure attainable and accessible housing. Thank you for your time and for letting me speak. Thank you. Mr. Michael Lacey. Good afternoon. Much of the documentary evidence cited in this audit request of OHS exists because I and other citizens fought to bring this information to light. Much of this evidence has been dismissed by senior Metro leadership as merely personality conflicts, misunderstandings fueled by the excessive passion of advocates for the unhoused. What's more, information from public records and reported by local media, including the Nashville scene and banner, has been called fake news by senior OHS leadership. But this request contains no reference to personality types or management styles. It does not include hearsay or rumors. Instead, you'll find direct citations to public records, financial statements, officially reported metrics, police reports, and discussion from the floor of Metro Council sessions. I'll ask you to do what anyone who sincerely wants the truth would ask. Please just examine the evidence. You're entitled to assume the worst of my intentions for speaking here today, but please examine the evidence. The relevant questions for you are simple. How was money spent and how is it supposed to be spent? What processes were meant to be followed and were they actually followed? What was meant to be accomplished and what was actually accomplished? We are not here today because mistakes were made or a few rules were bent for a greater purpose. 30 seconds. We are here because critical issues were not acknowledged. They appear to have been hidden. They went unaddressed. And the people who have the least power in the city, as is too often the case, seems to be the one paying the price. We all want to move forward. But to move forward, we must learn. And that begins with undertaking a simple, nonpartisan, bureaucratic thing that is not an assertion of wrongdoing, but merely an acknowledgement of accountability and routine oversight. Please perform a comprehensive audit of the Office of Homeless Services. All right, next part. Liz Maynard. Oh, I'm sorry. Steve Redner. Steve Redner. No, I switched to the five-day. We just moved everybody down. Okay, okay. Thank you so much. It's a good afternoon to everybody. I want to thank Mike Lacey for the work that he's done on this. I think there's, he's brought to attention some compliance and asset management issues. One of the issues that came up was that there were payments that were made on an expired contract. And that's a violation of policy. When Office of Homeless Services contracted with DePaul USA, it was for four months for operation and maintenance contract. I wanted to see a one-year operation and maintenance contract, not a four-month. And so what happened was, they paid it for four months, and they continued to pay on that contract. The problem is, we don't have a long-term contract. After four months, the vendor can go out there and double, triple the price if they want. Because you have people who are living over there. And when they're living there, what are you going to do? Have those people become displaced? I'm a big advocate for the homeless people. And I just think the way that was handled was really wrong. Mike did a really good job. I didn't know about any of this. I'm a general member. I'm a part of the COC general membership. I didn't know what was going on. I expect reports about what is happening to Strobel House. I just assumed, oh, I guess DePaul got an extension of their contract. I heard nothing. I was going to say, oh, I'm a big fan of the COC general membership. I didn't know what was going on until Mike Lacey went out there and made public records request and found out what was going on. And that really got me wound up and upset. I addressed the council. I think Angie Henderson is aware of what I said. I actually questioned the judgment and the leadership of Office of Homeless Services. This should not happen. And yet I don't know because what we have Metro accounting system does not monitor grant contracts until they're done. So that system is going to be changing. But for the Office of Homeless Services gets a lot of money through grant contracts, but they're only going to reviewed by the Metro Finance after they're completed. So where we're at right now is I'm supporting an audit. It doesn't have to be performance audit, but just a general audit. Thank you so much. Thank you. Thank you. Liz Maynard. Liz Maynard. I missed your question. I'm Liz Maynard. I am Vice Chair of the Homeless Planning Council, also lived experience. I will be five years sober. In December, I've been housed for five years now. I was homeless for over 10. Office of Homeless Services, I literally would not be here today. I didn't have the resources to obviously get housing or get any mentality to stay sober. When I had gone to the hospital and they said prepare your family, two weeks max, I was into roadway. I was getting bus passes to get to neighborhood health. I got referral, found out I had cirrhosis. I would have not been able to get any of that taken care of. Leaving, um, over there at Wallace, leaving there, I got my permanent housing and all the way through that, if I needed food, they were there. If I needed a bus pass, they were there. I had, you know, counseling, everything. They made sure the whole transition. They're not the office lights, go off, lock the door type of people. I have gotten phone calls on weekends to make sure I was okay and I had everything I need. They have literally saved my life. They saved so many. I think taking time to this, I'll like, every time we're, we're talking about something like this, one of my friends is dying out there. And so I just want to keep like, let's not put speed bumps or roadblocks any way, shape or form in their way of the work that they're doing because they're not, this isn't a number. A person is not a number. A person is a human being that could be lying on the sidewalk right now. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Dee Dee Bird. Yeah. Dee Dee Bird. I'm a, um, community advocate activist. I live in District 35, which was the home of Brookmead and Cammon before we got all those individuals housed. One of the things that I'm very concerned about is that just like Liz said, the work continues. Okay. Every department in Metro Nashville is audited. Every department we've called for an audit of Metro Parks multiple times. We have requested FOIA information multiple times because we too want to follow the money to make sure that people are doing their due diligence. I want to bring up the fact that the COC, which I'm a member of also as the general public, they were not able to, to put into place a group of people that could take care of the Strabble House. We had to bring someone from outside DePaul. The Salvation Army, the Salvation Army started the roadway in, which is where most of our individuals from Brookmead went after one year, they no longer wanted to do that service. So we had to bring in hospitality hub. And my point here is that the COC of Nashville is not capable of taking care of the big homeless issue that we have. And we have been watching this intently. And I've been in so many meetings. And one of the things that I have seen is CM Welsh, who's a dragged Jay Surveyor over the coals, which when he was the interim director, it was the most humiliating thing I've ever seen. These people are doing hard work. It is fluid. It changes every day. It is about human beings. And the fact that we're standing here today in front of you, discussing an audit for monetary figures that change because my point was that Salvation Army couldn't do that job anymore. We had to bring in somebody else. It changes every year. Sometimes it changes. every four months. That's why they wanted a four month contract. They didn't know what they were getting into. They'd never been to Nashville before. We had to bring in outside help. So I think there are other ways to deal with this than this type of audit by someone who has continuously wanted to make problems for the Office of Home and Services. Thank you. Thank you. That's it. That's it. I was going to contribute for your comments today. Thank you. Thank you. Next item on the agenda is the approval of the minutes from the previous meeting. Do we hear a motion? So moved. Second. All in favor? Aye. Any opposed? Motion carries. Old business? Yes. Our item on old business. Yes. So if you'll remember, we carry forward the Nashville General Hospital investigation to each agenda as we follow the remediation of those recommendations that were made through that investigation. Within your workbook, there is a matrix of the recommendations and the related allegations. If you see a yes, that means not only has General Hospital taken the steps to remediate and address that recommendation, but it also means our lead investigator, Paul, has gone out and actually verified that it is actually remediated. There is only one left. The one that is left relates to the physician that was utilizing space and services of Nashville General Hospital without an agreement in place. The reason that this one is still open is because they are still trying to quantify the amount, like square footage and the individuals for the self-reported start violation that they are putting together. Once that happens, that is when that one will be closed. But other than that, they are making headway. As you all saw, they recently signed a new PSA with Meharry. And Dr. Elders, their interim CEO, has worked very close with Paul to make sure that all of these are getting addressed. Are there any questions? Question, Mayor. Chair, on this material we have here regarding the lawsuit for the overbilling by City Ballet that was filed in August of 2025, I didn't know if we could just have sort of a status report on that. Will we anticipate the timeline for that being? We don't have a timeline for that. We are just aware that the lawsuit has been filed in all honesty. Past that legal information, we don't have. We just know that they're pursuing the refunding of that overpayment. Okay. And if I may, Chair, I have three questions. For the remediated issue around contract signatures and some of the backdating and not signing and some of those issues, I think I had elevated this in a previous meeting just from a continuity of process standpoint and consistency across all our Metro departments. I'm seeing here that DocuSign has been purchased for use on all contracts. I apologize if I don't remember the answer to this prior, but I had wondered why, as a Metro government, we do not have kind of like an enterprise contract for DocuSign, either held by General Services, finance, or legal. And literally, if you are within Metro government, you use DocuSign full stop. And like, why is like the hospital authority buying DocuSign and this department's buying DocuSign? Can anybody speak to that? I mean, correct me if I'm wrong, but since General Hospital is its own component entity, it does not utilize the same contracts that Metro government has. It's kind of like when we're looking into the financial contract that they're using for assistance, piggybacking off of ours and whether or not that's allowed is my understanding, is that they do have to have their own standalone contracts. Okay. Is that correct, director? That is correct regarding DocuSign for the hospital. Okay. And would that be true for any of our other kind of authorities? Very. It's a great question. And we can definitely look into that, vice mayor, as to, because I am not sure of the answer as to why the entirety of Metro, which I think is your question, does not use DocuSign. And it is definitely by department. So, but we can look into that and report back to you. I appreciate that. And then I think the last question. Nope, that was it. Thank you. Thank you. Can I just add real quick about General Hospital? We have been working with them. Finance has been working with General Hospital as well as their contractor for accounting services. And I will report that has been going really, really well. And so I just wanted to report that that has been smooth. We have had a lot of transparent, honest conversations back and forth about their accounting. And it looks like their close for FY25 is. So. Thank you. Thank you. Good news. New business. New business. So the first three items under new business are somewhat lumped together. As you know, we do have the request for the audit for the Office of Homeless Services. Typically when we have audit requests, the committee asks about other work that's been done in our office related to that. We just happened to have just issued two follow-up reports that touched on homeless services. The caveat being that when these audits were done, one's an investigation, one's an audit. They were underneath social services at the time. This was prior to Office of Homeless Services becoming a standalone department. We have not audited those. But I'll start with the investigation. Back in 2024, we issued an investigative report into allegations of contracts at social services. There were two allegations related to this. One had to do with wasteful spending on a contract for services not rendered. And then the other one had to do with utilizing services by an outside vendor or an out-of-state vendor when a local vendor could have been utilized. Both of these allegations were unsubstantiated, but there were two recommendations that came out of that investigation, which is typical for our investigations. The first one was recouping funds that were overpaid to the vendor. There were some unallowable costs as well as one invoice had something that was double billed almost. But it was about $1,500. So the recommendation there was to try to reach out to the vendor and recoup those funds. That attempt was made. The overpayment was reimbursed. What social services, which we may have to get Director Pratt if there's any questions related to this because she's in the other room. The second piece of it was unallowable expenses that were requested for reimbursement from the vendor. Unfortunately, what the old CFO at social services did was he told the vendor that that was okay. And so the vendor never repaid them when they reached out. So recently, social services reached out again to ask for repayment. And they came to an agreement with the vendor that since the amount of time that has passed since that payment was made and since the old CFO told them it was allowed, that they decided not to pursue getting the other $1,100-ish back. So that was the first recommendation. The second recommendation was to put a process in place so that that doesn't happen again, making sure those invoices are compared to contracts so that any payments that are made, they're not overpayments and they're not paying on allowable expenses. We verified that a process was put into place and that it was operating so both of those were considered implemented. Are there any questions on the investigation? Okay. The next one was we did an audit of the Homeless Impact Division, which was what Homeless Services was before it moved out from underneath social services. We did this one. We issued it in 2023, which was right before it became its own standalone department. But with that, when Office of Homeless Services became its own department, these recommendations followed it to the actual department. The audit itself looked at a number of things. It looked at the governance of the Homeless Planning Council. It looked at the security of the data that they were collecting. And it looked at their processes for coordinated entry and other processes they had in place for effectiveness. That audit resulted in seven recommendations. These recommendations, kind of lumping them together, some of them were related to securing data and running some reports to make sure that the data administration is secured. Documenting minutes to our Homeless Planning Council meetings. And also making an encampment strategy as well as an encampment team and some other pieces that were there. Six out of seven of them were fully implemented. The one that was not fully implemented and was partially implemented related to HUD has some required policies and procedures that are supposed to be in the organization's operating manual. At the time of our initial audit, 11 of them, 11 out of 23, were not in that manual. At the time of our follow-up audit, five were still not in that manual. So that one was partially implemented. I will note that since that audit follow-up came out in July, those five have been added. And as of September 10th, they were approved by the Homeless Planning Council within that manual. So that one now, we have not verified it. We have not seen it. So I won't say it's completely closed, but it has been reported as being implemented. Are there any questions on that follow-up? Could you just restate that last part? As of September 10th, the meeting of the Homelessness Planning Council, those five remaining things were included on? Were included in the new manual that gets approved by the Planning Council. Okay, yeah. Lauren, once you verify this, you will report back to the committee too. Okay, thank you. It won't be a standalone report, but it would be actually reported back as being closed. Okay, thank you. Okay. Next item. Okay. So this flows into our next item, which is the request, the audit request for the Office of Homeless Services. Within each of your workbooks, you have the initial request from Council Member Welsh that states the concerns, financial and operational concerns relating to the Office of Homeless Services, as well as you also have a separate packet yesterday and into today. We did receive a number of emails supporting this audit, and so we've printed them out for each of you to have in review. And so with that, I will turn it back over for your decision on how you want to dismiss. Yes. Okay. So would you like to make some comment? Yes, I would, if I could. Okay. Wait. Wait. Sorry. I'm sorry. No, you go. Well, I just wanted to add that I believe that last time we had a similar situation where you wished to hear from one or more persons regarding a specific request for an audit, and the way you entertained that before, you had a motion to decide to have a hearing, and you set time limits for how long you'd like to hear from each person who would be speaking, and that was all rolled into one motion. So. Last time, Chair, it was also five minutes per person, which, I mean, just for the record. So we'll entertain a motion. So. Second. Yeah, I will second that motion. All in favor? Aye. So we will allow each of you to speak for five minutes. Thank you so much. I really appreciate the opportunity to come before you today to talk about my request for an audit. You all have the packet in hand that details many of the reasons that I think underscore the need for an audit, so I'm not going to repeat those here. But I do want to call attention to two overarching issues that I believe warrant a comprehensive examination of this department at this time. And the first centers on finance and a lack of compliance with financial policies, potentially not acting responsibly in accordance with the law, and a lack of transparency within the department around these issues. And those, again, are underscored in the document that I gave. The recent debacle with the DePaul contract at Strobel House underscores this. OHS continued to pay invoices despite those invoices making it obvious that the numbers did not add up. They referred to a contract that was expired, but the amount of the contract on the invoice was triple what the actual contract was. So the question is, what else are they not aware of? Can we trust any of these numbers that we're getting from them if there's such a disconnect between what is actually happening on the ground and what they think is happening on the ground? I specifically asked the director about this at a committee meeting, and she said there were two contracts and they just got confused and didn't realize that a contract had expired, so that gives me pause. The second area is ethics. The ARP funding that we received was specifically directed towards implementing a housing-first policy to address homelessness. But the question is, are we doing housing-first? Are people being referred to in a timely manner when we have available permanent and temporary housing options, and why or why not? I would say they are not. What happens when a landlord gives back money? We don't know. Why are we keeping beds open for over a year when we have people on the street who need those beds? Is what is happening really housing-first, and is it in line with our understanding of what an ethical, person-centered, housing-focused approach is? I would argue no, but I believe that is a question for the auditor to determine. In the ordinance that created this department, OHS's role was outlined as coordinating and bringing people together, but instead we're hearing distrust from the very community partners that OHS is tasked to bring it together. At the most recent meeting of the HPC, the community's CE procedures you referred to earlier were voted on after months of discussion. But at the last minute, the very last minute, OHS sent in a document contradicting the entire CE procedure document put together by a COC committee. Fortunately, OHS's recommendations were not adopted, but the question is, why were they so aggressively, I would say, divisive? I really believe that we need answers to these questions. I believe an audit is warranted to help our community understand how Metro has implemented millions of dollars designated towards homelessness. An audit could be a first step toward restoring trust. It will help our community improve on what we're doing. We are at a critical point where millions of dollars in homelessness funding is going away. We have to create more transparency and open discourse to rebuild a system that has not worked based on the endpoint I and my colleagues have received from our constituents. If you don't look at this, we cannot improve on what we're doing, and we cannot provide a full range of services to the people that deserve those services. And finally, I would say Metro has a policy that any recipient of $750,000 in federal fundings are required to undergo a single audit to ensure appropriate financial controls and program compliance. Metro as a whole is audited under this Single Audit Act, but the departments are not. But Metro's grant manual requires compliance with a single audit act, so any Metro grant recipient of more than $750,000 of ARP or other federal funding dollars has to undergo an audit. And we make nonprofits do this, which can cost a nonprofit upwards of $50,000 to do it. So if we are requiring nonprofits to undergo this audit, and other departments within Metro, like Metro Transit goes through, MDHA goes through this audit, which I believe is ethically and legally correct, I think that our departments should be held to the very same standard. We are in danger with this particular administration if we find that these monies have been misspent of having this money clawed back. And I think that an audit would assure everyone that these monies have actually been spent in the way that they are required to be spent, and that we can rest easy knowing that when we lose this funding, that we will be able to continue and build the system with new funding that comes in, with everyone knowing that the dollars are being used appropriately and in the way that best addresses the needs of our unhoused population. Thank you so much. Thank you. Hello. Hello. Thank you all for having me. Director April Calvin, the Director of the Office of Homeless Services. One, I'd like to say thank you for having us, and thank you for your time. OHS is pretty much an open book. We are open to audits. We're open to questions. I'm proud to reveal that in the last three years, we've been through a number of the audits that you've discussed today, and we actually just completed a single audit. Thank you for reminding me of that. We just completed a single audit in our department as well, so departments do actually go through single audits annually as well. There's four chairs. There's four chairs if you guys want to come in. Thank you. Can y'all consider? One, two, three, four, don't worry. I'm just wondering if you're excited. All right. Well, good afternoon. It's nice to be with you all today. Our office recently issued an investigative report related to the Davidson County Clerk's Office. Real quick, I think it's important, though. We've got some important people. We've got Ms. Winn, who is a county clerk. The way this kind of unfolded, you had a person at the county clerk's office who saw something that was suspicious. They notified management of that suspicious activity. There is a law that, you know, they went in there and they started doing their due diligence to see, you know, what was going on. When they got to a point where they felt there could be potential fraud, they reported to the state just like they should have. So that's something to, one, that you had an employee who reported the suspicious activity. Two, that you had a department that followed through on the law and contacted the state. The state contacted us and then we said, Paul, which we appreciate Paul did all the work. We appreciate the work that he did. So, to put it simply, it deals with the misappropriation of cash. You have two different licenses that we're going to be talking about. You've got a standard business license and then you've got a minimal activity business license. The main difference between the two, if you're a business, is how much revenue you bring in. So if it's over $100,000, you do a standard business license. If it's under $100,000, you do a minimal activity license. For the purposes of this investigation, distinguishing factors would include, if it's a minimal activity license, whether it's the, you know, you're getting the application for the first time or you're getting a renewal, all that has to be handled by the Davidson County Clerk's Office. They take the cash. And the system will not print that license without there being cash recorded into the system. And then later down the line, part of their closeout procedures will be matching, reconciling what was recorded in the system versus what cash they actually have in front of them. If it's a standard business license, if it's the initial application, that will be handled by the Davidson County Clerk's Office. However, if it's any subsequent renewal, that is paid to the Department of Revenue directly to the state. But there are some customers who want to come in. They don't have the printer capabilities or whatnot. So they can't print the license. So they will go into the Davidson County Clerk's Office to print the license. But there's no money exchange, so there's nothing put into the system. Well, basically what happens, you had a staff member there. They were able to manipulate the system. And somebody would come in for a minimal activity license, okay? They're supposed to make a payment. But they could manipulate the system as if it were a standard business license. So no money was recorded into the system. They could print the license. That person could take the money. And since it's not recorded in the system, it's not going to be part of the reconciliation process. So Paul went out there, and they were helpful in terms of trying to figure out what happened, how much money was stolen. Couldn't totally get a great feel on how much because there were some limitations in terms of the type of work that you could do. But basically they were able to confirm through video cameras that the person was taking money from certain customers, certain businesses, but there was no corresponding entry into the system. So it was substantiated. That person resigned back in November, I think, of 2024. They had put some controls in place. One of them, they're working with the software vendor to make it where if it is a minimum activity license, you cannot put into the system that it's a standard business license. They're working with that. They've hired a position that's basically going to serve as kind of like an external, like an extra set of eyes in terms of they're going to do spot checks on, you know, going through the cameras, making sure policies and procedures are being formed, that sort of thing. And they're also working with the vendor. One of the issues that was you could not reconcile the state business license, what was printed versus what money was actually being received by the state. That was very difficult. So they're working to resolve it that way. That's it in a nutshell in terms of very short and sweet, but we're happy to answer any questions that you have. Questions? At the risk of oversimplifying this, is there a reason we're still accepting cash payments for these things? It seems like that would do away with the problem. My understanding, y'all may be able to speak to this more than we can, but a lot of times your citizens, that's the only way that they can pay. I wish we didn't have to take cash. But there are people who insist on paying only with cash or who want to write checks. People come into our office to write a check so they don't have to pay the 2% fee. And again, if I could say no cash, only card transactions, I absolutely would. But I don't know that I would be serving the public interest to say, you can't pay me in any other way except with a card, because what that entails is them having to pay an additional 2%. I appreciate that. It just seems like more and more of a common practice that we... I know. ...places are all that are in cash. And since you do have the option of paying a check to avoid that... I absolutely wish I could go that way. Were these proposed software changes, where they can't cross the line between the... Yes. I don't know what you're trying to... Basically, you could go in and manipulate the system to turn it into a standard business license. Or at least print the standard business license without the system expecting a payment. Because if it's a minimal activity license, the system is expecting a payment before it's going to print anything. So what will happen in a situation where the previous year they used the minimal, but they crossed the threshold to require a full... What happened is that the state changed the threshold. There used to be a time when minimal activity was 3 to 10,000, and the state increased it to the 100,000. So some of these people already had that standard business license because they did business over the $10,000 threshold. And so it's our belief that that change kind of caused a problem... help will cause the problem because folks started looking for the business licenses on May 15th. And if I had a standard business license on May 15th, I would just get one in the mail. But if I didn't get mine, I'd walk into the office and get one. And that was part of what happened. Did I get that right, Tammy? The supervisor override. Well, and then what we've asked for with the new system, for the software system, is that any time there's a change in the type of business license, that it would require supervisor approval. Employee can't change anything. The supervisor would have to come in and give the approval to have the business license change from a standard to a minimal or vice versa. Questions for Clerk Wynn. So the change that you were speaking to at this... was at the state as to what amount of business constituted the different types of licenses. And it just changed, yeah. When was that point of change? It was January 24th. 24th. January 24th. Okay. So, and was this employee employed at that time? They were. They were. Doing this task? Yes. In particular. Okay. So while we could, from camera, deduce on October 22nd, 24th, November 1, November 12, we might, it'd be speculation, but given that kind of threshold moment in November of 2024, for the fact that the person who was formerly employed was doing this task, we might presume that in that intervening time, this was happening or could have been happening. Could have been. Okay. Okay. And I guess my last question goes a little bit more to, generally when, whether for cash exchange or some of these smaller actions, when a particular employee is found to have been conducting, you know, fraud, malfeasance, or otherwise, that person resigned. So I know if that person moves to another county, tries to work at the county clerk or otherwise, or in that, I know what they call you clerk, when you're not giving them a good reference, right? You're going to be real clear. But I do wonder when we have folks in Metro government who resign, does their record reflect why they resign so they don't go to another municipality and perpetrate a similar fraud? If they were to be fired for cause, their record would show that. But can anybody speak to, from an HR perspective, what happens there? I don't know about the HR side of it. We can ask about that. Yeah, we could have a follow-up on that because I, yeah, I am concerned that when over recent years, as we have elevated something that we cannot substantiate beyond a specific window of time, but we have reason to believe that it happened for many and many years, and if they just go and go and work in another government, like how are we making sure that they're not going to perpetrate that or use the experience that they learned here to do that to another government. So I'd like to understand that, please. Thank you. Any other questions or comments on that issue? No. Okay. Thank you for being here. Thank you. And just know that we take very seriously the responsibility we have to collect and preserve, protect revenue on behalf of the state and the county, and just know that we will continue to do our best to protect all the revenue we collect. Thank you. Thank you so much. Thank you. Thank you. Next we have our external auditors, Crossland, presenting the external audit plan for 2025. This is typically done in June. We moved it to September since we knew there might be some turnover on the audit committee. Thank you. Thank you. Good afternoon. Again, I'm John Crossland. I will go through the plan. As Lauren just said, that we normally would have done this in summertime, early summer or something. But we are underway in the audit now. But I'm going to go through and show you what our plan is. And we are executing that plan now. On page one is the agenda. And these are kind of the items I'm going to talk about. I'll go through. If you have any questions, please stop me. I won't take very long. I know we have a full agenda today. But any questions, stop me, ask me. I'd be happy to. Page two is our engagement team members. We do have a few changes on here. We do have a few changes on here. But this also, Mark England, he's over here. He's the overall audit manager. Last year we had Katie. Mark's been on the audit for a number of years and has moved into that role. We're happy about that. We do have one new audit manager on the hospital, J.D. Cage. He's not here. But he's the new manager on there. I think everybody else. We've shuffled around, myself. And we've brought Erica Sager, who's been an audit partner of ours for 20 years. She's on Metro Water and Sewer. And Jennifer Montrenak is then, she's a concurring reviewer on a few of these areas this year. So we do try to give it a fresh look as we go through year by year. And we rotate around so we have enough partners and enough managers, luckily, to be able to do that. And so we... Can I ask one question? Absolutely. For your audit manager on the hospital, could you maybe speak a little bit to his experience? Do you play in the hospital arena? Yes. He has been with us for six or seven years. He has not been on this hospital audit. This is his first year, as it is mine, actually, the first year. I'm the principal in charge of it. We both have some health care experience, and we've been around this hospital audit. I've probably done independent reviews on it in the past and dealt with major issues. But we're both new. So we're getting... It's a whole new staff over there, and it's a whole new staff on our side. And so far, it's gone really well. I mean... Because of their new staff, your new staff, do you see that as a higher level of risk in the audit this time? Yeah. I mean, we adjust our risk for that, absolutely. But, you know, we figure out how to compensate for that through our audit procedures, and we're doing so. We're actually in the third week of field work right now already. So we're well... We're at least halfway through the audit now, through the field work part. All right. Thank you for that job. Yeah, great question. Page three is our responsibilities. We like to lay out what the auditor's responsibilities. It is an external financial statement audit. The word audit is loosely used for many, many things, especially today. There's internal audit projects. There's monitoring versus auditing. There's external audit. This is an external audit of the ACFER. And so our responsibilities are to express opinions about whether the financial statements prepared by management under the oversight of this audit committee are fairly presented in all material respects. We don't audit without exception. We audit to materiality. And that it's in conformity with GAAP. Not only GAAP, but government auditing standards. I came in here a minute ago and talked about uniform guidance. There's a yellow book right there. I have some funny stories of why that covers yellow for another day. But the uniform guidance is the single audit. And it is a compliance audit by the federal government that we follow those rules and regulations and have a separate contract to audit with the state for those procedures. Our responsibilities are to also report back to management and this audit committee if we have any material weaknesses, if we have any significant deficiencies, and, of course, if we have any noncompliance within the single audit. And, of course, if we detect or find any fraud. Management, it is their report. It's their ACFER. They're in charge of drafting the report, of adopting the proper accounting policies of which we audit and making sure compliance with GAAP. Establishing and maintaining internal controls, which I've heard a lot talk about internal controls here. Preventing and detecting fraud. Disclosing to this audit committee and to us if they detect any fraud. So we can adjust our audit scope when it comes to the external audit. Next page is independence. Rule 101, AICPA's Code of Professional Conduct requires us, and government audit standards, requires us to be independent. In fact, in appearance. And we are. Next page five is fraud risk. That's covered under SAS 99. This is not a forensic audit. But there are certain high-risk areas that we do audit concerning fraud risk and whether that could impact the financial statements in a material way. There's four-pronged strategy that we basically use that's stipulated in SAS 99. Gather information. That is brainstorming amongst ourselves. Where are these high-risk areas of fraud? A lot of that comes through our inquiries of not only the management at the finance department, but internal audit, whether it be whatever department, whether it be a constitutional office like the clerk's office. We ask various people amongst all the different divisions of Metro and come up with identified risk. That's one of the other prongs. And then we test for management override. And then we evaluate all that evidence. And that helps bring us to our focus on where those high-risk areas are. And then we either substantially audit, substantively audit it, or audit the controls surrounding those areas. The next page is our methodology, overall methodology and approach. We have it here in a flow chart. And then on the next page, in written form, the audit, planning, and a risk assessment. I kind of talked about it with fraud. But our goal is to find and identify where we think there are high-risk areas of material misstatement. And that is where our focus is during the external audit. Right now, management override of controls and improper revenue recognition, those are kind of always high-risk areas, especially for government. So when we look at testing, like I said before, we do certain areas where we test controls and certain areas where we do substantive testing. On the bottom of page 7 here, we've kind of put some examples of what those are. So controls, we're going to test cash receipts, property tax billings, employee comp, bank recs, those kind of items where we can test to see that we believe there are strong controls surrounding it. And we're able to test those areas. And we're able to test that those controls are intact and properly functioning. And therefore, we can rely on all the work that underlies those controls. Substantive testing, sometimes it just makes more sense if you have hundreds of millions of dollars of investments just to confirm it with the brokerage firm or a cash account. And that's when you get into substantive testing. You can see some of those areas there, especially when you get to the hospital, third-party settlements, patient accounts receivable, things like that. The next page I kind of touched on earlier is the single audit. I won't go through the 20% and the calculation and all that. But based on last year's CIFA, which is the statement that says what all the federal expenditures are, because those major programs that we determine, it's not based on revenue. It's not based on the total grant awarded. It's based on the actual expenditures under that grant for the year. And so we don't have a final CIFA yet, nor have we still don't, right? Nor would we expect to have it yet. But if we did, these are the programs that we're kind of guessing that we'll test as major programs. Who provides the CIFA and what does that acronym stand for? Catherine. Catherine and Donna. Catherine and Donna provide the CIFA for us. And the statement expenditures for federal rewards. I didn't know who. A lot of people get it to it. Management gets it. But there's different departments that includes, like, you might be a better one day. So finance provides them with the expenditures out of the grants and a certain threshold in the year, and then that informs. They'll give us a full listing of all federal expenditures, whether it's subject to audit. I mean, everything's subject to audit. The full, full. The departments report. The different departments have to report to finance. That's what I was trying to figure out. I didn't know if you were asking that or not. So every year, finance will do it before the audit begins. We do a year-end training. We also have a single audit training that we roll out to all the departments to talk about. Here's what you need to send in for single audit and what the single audit is, and we try and educate folks on the single audit. Then we receive information from the various departments. We also match that. OFA actually keeps a database of all the grant contracts that have come in. So we do some matching to say, did this department report to us correctly? And we say, yes, that matches with the database that OFA collects. We are working to actually procure a system that will help automate some of this instead of it being in a database. Access database. Access database. Access database. It will actually be in software that will help us a little bit to wrap our arms around it, and it'll make it a lot more efficient, if you will. So that's how that works. And then finance, once they gather all the information from the departments, they will put it into an Excel spreadsheet and all of the information. They send it to the auditors and then turn it over to them for the audit process. Got it. Thank you. Okay. Okay. Yeah. Okay. Next page is prior year issues and recommendations. We didn't have any material weaknesses or significant deficiencies in the prior year or compliance findings. So we did have some management letter comments of which we went over with the committee, but nothing that would affect this single audit threshold, which we've had in the past. Congratulations. Yeah. That's good. Here, page 11, we've issued just new statements. We actually had a call today on GASB 101 compensated absences. That will have an effect on this year's ACFER and management's on top of that, and it'll be properly reported. So can I elaborate just a little bit on what compensated absences are? So at Metro, we accrue sick time, and so that would be a compensated absence. So in the past, we have not been required under GASB to accrue those at the government-wide financial statement level. But this year, we will be accruing those. So, and it will result in a prior period adjustment as well. So I just, we know that's coming. That's not a, oh my gosh, you had a prior period adjustment. It's just part of the GASB and implementing this GASB 101 this year. You have vacation time as well, sick time and vacation time. So we've done, we've been doing vacation time. That's already been. This is just for. This adds. This adds to that accrual. Okay. Sick time for, estimated sick time that it will be used. Yes. Which is really complicated. It is. It's a lot. Yeah. Yeah. And we didn't record it previously because we don't pay out our sick. Right. When people leave, we don't pay it out. Right. So we don't want to, didn't want to accrue it. But now, since GASB is saying we have to, we are making a calculation to, that's determined. The viewing public GASB is, and myself, because I can't, I know what it is, but I can't. General accounting standards. General accounting standards. Governmental. Governmental. So the for-profit and non-profit world follows FASB, and the government's version is GASB. GASB. Yes. Understood. Thank you. Sure. 102 is just a reporting standard. We'll make sure that there's nothing in there that'll affect. There might be one more sentence. I mean, when GASB was created in, I think, 1984, it kind of cut FASB off and said, government just can't follow that anymore. But there are some loose ends that are finally being tied up. And so that's just clarification reporting. 103 and 104 will not be applicable this year. It'll be 26. But my guess is there will be, there definitely will be, 103 will affect, I mean, it'll affect every government, but it's just reporting. It's not counting, just reporting. And then 104 is just enhanced disclosures on capital assets. Is that like- Mainly intangibles, right of use assets, new considered assets that haven't been exactly covered on how to disclose. Okay. Okay. Yeah. Page 12 is our general timeline of, you know, we've been out working central government since the summer, mainly testing controls. Kind of our timeline of when during the year. And I think we'll, right so far, right now, we're on schedule. September looks to be the month when you're doing all the things for this graph. We're very busy right now. Yes. Laura, our next meeting is December. Yes. And that will be the meeting where we will- Have the draft and executive session. 12 is just the anticipated completion if everything goes as planned for all the different deliverables. And then we have our contacts, page 13. I can answer any questions. I want to ask a quick follow-up question to Chair Bates' question. So we will have two meetings in December. One in executive session to review the act firm, right? And then we will have a second one where we actually accept, we don't approve it, accept the annual comprehensive financial report. because it will be filed by 12-31. We're on the same page. Congratulations, Mark, by the way. Thank you, John. Sure. Would you all kindly leave one extra copy as well for the council office? You can just put it on the edge of the table right there. I'll make sure to get it when I go. Thank you so much. Yes. You said that. Annual comprehensive financial report. Our next item. Is it going to be accessible? Yes. So annually- Internally for our office, we do a self-assessment to make sure that we're following yellow book standards. And also we do an annual assessment of the audit committee to make sure that we're following working with critical feedback and health protection in our office. You're doing an annual assessment of the audit committee to make sure that we're following good job of giving us an existing financial report. That's right. If you don't get here. If you don't get out of time, do you want to call me the policy or let me get out of as much other eye contact by doing this? Okay. How are you doing to call me? Okay. How are you doing to call me? All right. Well, this is going to be able to call me a report and get out of all of your audience. assessment of the audit committee to make sure that the audit committee is meeting the bylaws that you all have set forth. This is kind of an accountability reporting since our office tends to do and manage most of these items it's accountability for you all to see that we are making sure that those bylaws are met. This year was all green again. Basically it means that you met the appropriate amount of times, you met with the external auditors the appropriate amount of times, you accepted the external document, external audit documents as required by the bylaws, you did my performance evaluation, we posted minutes, we posted agendas correctly, and we adjusted the audit plan as needed and you all heard our reporting of all of the audit reports that we did. So each of these was done appropriately. So that's... Okay, next two items. I'll go through these kind of quick since it's taken a while. Recommendation implementation. We actually had 51 recommendations that were due this time. Thirty-three of them were reported as implemented. The bulk of those is Arts Commission. They have been working very hard to get all of those recommendations implemented as fast as they can. We're hoping that by 2026 audit plan we will have them back on our audit plan to do that follow-up audit with them or that full audit of them again. The one that needed a revised date, 18 of them, they were all disaster recovery business continuity report. Since that report is redacted I did not put them in the audit committee workbook since you couldn't have seen the recommendations anyway. Basically they are working towards each and every one of those but they were dependent on a consultant for the first piece of this but took a little longer than expected expected so it has pushed the recommendation implementation they've asked to extend it to the end of the year but those are being implemented. Any questions on that? I apologize. When you say they, so disaster recovery and business continuity that's what we're talking about? OEM, yes. OEM, okay thank you. Okay, next is our ongoing projects. We've got a handful of projects that are in draft reporting right now. We are working our way through that audit plan. It did just change a little bit but we are working our way through it. We've got staff assigned to certain projects and kind of have figured out how the end of the year is going to go as we work towards that. We also issued two investigation reports this year and we've received hotline calls and emails and other methods. One thing that we're very proud of is we're working with ITS to put together that Metro-wide training on fraud, waste and abuse. They are putting together that video for us. Paul has done a great job of writing a script for it to get it put together so we're hoping that that will increase our calls to a fraud, waste and abuse even more. That's fabulous. Yeah, it's important. It really is. It's really proud of you. Paul is doing it. Paul is doing it. Yes, thank you. It's important. The budget, we are under budget. One of the main reasons we are currently under budget is because we still have that open position that we received last year for the investigator two position. We are not the only department that wanted to post a position at the beginning of the fiscal year so it took a little bit longer to get it posted. It has closed. We just got the list of candidates today and so we are hoping to interview them quickly and get that position filled. That's the main reason we're under budget. It kind of looks like we're not spending our consulting budget but I will tell you that we already have almost every dollar of that assigned to a project. With the addition of changes to the audit plan, we've had to utilize those funds pretty much all of them already. So they will be fully used this year which in the past we haven't completely used them so we're really excited to actually fulfill that budget this time around. And that staffing, like I said, we have that one open position. We're hoping to get it filled and onboarded because we do have a staff member who is retiring at the end of the year and we're hoping that we will have that position ready to be filled when he retires. That's all. Does that, yeah I'm sorry, will that keep the number of empties at 12? Yes. Any other administrative matters? Any considerations for our next meeting that we discuss? One thing I will all throw out there, since we've recently had a number of recommendations, requests to change the audit plan, our office would like to put policy around it to determine the best course of action instead of each meeting us kind of figuring out. And so we will be bringing that to y'all at one of the meetings in December. We're going to probably have to ask Metro Legal what the parameters are and kind of look at some other instances as we enjoy getting requests. It's a great opportunity for us to find impactful audits but also making sure that they're consistently applied and how we handle those. We look forward to that. With that, I will declare the public meeting adjourned. Great. Thank you. impressions employees employees employees employees employees employees

SCOPE
The Metropolitan Nashville Audit Committee is to ensure that
the
Metropolitan Government of Nashville and Davidson County (Metropolitan
Nashville Government) has effective, efficient, and sustainable internal
controls over its major risks.
To the extent permitted by the Metropolitan Charter the Metropolitan
Nashville Audit Committee is authorized to conduct
financial audits,
performance audits, or other audit services including investigation and
fraud concerning any department,
disposition of reported incidents of

the

Financial Statements
• While the financial statement audit engagement is ongoing meet in
executive session with the external auditor near the mid-point of the
audit engagement and prior to final issuance of the comprehensive
annual financial report, to review progress, including any difficulties
encountered, with the audit engagement and follow-up as appropriate.
• Review final audit reports and accept, or not accept, the audit results.
• Review with Metropolitan Nashville Government management and the
external auditors all matters requiring communication to the Committee
under generally accepted auditing standards.

• Understand the scope of internal and external auditors' reviews of
