Note 1—Nature of organization and significant accounting policies (continued) 
Land,  Building,  and  Equipment  –  RITI  capitalizes  all  expenditures  for  land,  building,  and  equipment  in  excess  of 
$1,000. Purchases of land, building, and equipment are carried at cost. Donated property and equipment are carried 
at the approximate fair value at the date of donation. Depreciation is computed using the straight-line method over 
estimated useful lives of 5 to 39 years. 
Income Taxes – RITI is exempt from federal income taxes under Section 501(c)(3) of the Internal Revenue Code, 
and  is not a  private  foundation.  Accordingly, no provision  for income  taxes  has been made  in the  accompanying 
financial statements. 
RITI  follows  FASB  ASC  guidance  related  to  unrecognized  tax  benefits.  The  guidance  clarifies  the  accounting  for 
uncertainty  in  income  taxes  recognized  in  an  organization’s  financial  statements.  This  guidance  prescribes  a 
minimum probability threshold that a tax position must meet before a financial statement benefit is recognized. The 
minimum threshold is defined as a tax position that is more likely than not to be sustained upon examination by the 
applicable taxing authority, including resolution of any related appeals or litigation processes, based on the technical 
merits of the position. The tax benefit to be recognized is measured as the largest amount of benefit that is greater 
than  50%  likely  of  being  realized  upon  ultimate  settlement.  RITI  has  no  tax  penalties  or  interest  reported  in  the 
accompanying financial statements.  
Use  of  Estimates  –  The  preparation  of  financial  statements  in  conformity  with  accounting  principles  generally 
accepted in the United States of America (“U.S. GAAP”) requires management to make estimates and assumptions 
that affect the reported amounts of assets and liabilities and disclosure of contingent assets and liabilities at the date 
of the financial statements and the reported amounts of revenues and expenses during the reporting period. Actual 
results could differ from those estimates. 
Contributed  Materials  and  Services  –  Contributed  materials  and  equipment,  if  any,  are  reflected  as  contributed 
nonfinancial assets in the accompanying financial statements at their estimated values at the date of receipt. 
Contributed use of facilities is recorded at the estimated fair market value. 
Contributions of donated services that create or enhance nonfinancial assets or that require specialized skills, are 
provided  by  individuals  possessing  those  skills,  and  would  typically  need  to  be  purchased  if  not  provided  by 
donation, are recorded at their fair values in the period received.  
Additionally,  a  number  of  non-professional  volunteers  donated  approximately  21,900  and  9,984  hours  during  the 
years  ended  June  30,  2022  and  2021,  respectively,  to  RITI’s  program  services.  However,  these  services  do  not 
meet the requirements above and have not been recorded. 
Functional Allocation of Expenses – The costs of providing program and other activities have been summarized 
on a functional basis in the statements of activities. While most costs have been directly assigned to a functional 
category,  certain  joint  costs  have  been  allocated  among  program  services  and  supporting  services  benefited. 
Such  allocations  are  determined  by  management  on  an  equitable  basis.  Expenses  that  are  allocated  consist 
primarily of salaries and wages expense which is allocated based on time and effort.

Recently  Adopted  Accounting  Pronouncements  –  In  September  2020,  FASB  issued  Accounting  Standards 
Update  (“ASU”)  2020-07,  Presentation  and  Disclosures  by  Not-for-Profit  Entities  for  Contributed  Nonfinancial 
Assets.  This  ASU  requires  not-for-profit  entities  to  present  contributed  nonfinancial  assets  as  a  separate  line 
item  in  the  statement  of  activities,  apart  from  contributions  of  cash  and  other  financial  assets.  In  addition,  for 
each  category  of  contributed  nonfinancial  assets  recognized,  certain  additional  disclosures  are  required.  This 
standard is effective for the year ending June 30, 2022. There have been no donor restrictions placed on such 
contributions. 
Accounting Policies for Future Pronouncements – In February 2016, FASB issued ASU 2016-02, Leases. The 
standard requires all leases with lease terms over 12 months to be capitalized as a right-of-use asset and lease 
liability on the statement of financial position at the date of lease commencement. Leases will be classified as 
either  finance  or  operating.  This  distinction  will  be  relevant  for  the  pattern  of  expense  recognition  in  the 
statement of activities. This standard will be effective for the fiscal year ending June 30, 2023. RITI is currently 
evaluating the effect of the implementation of this new standard. 
Subsequent  Events  –  RITI  has  evaluated  subsequent  events  and  transactions  through  January  10,  2023,  the 
date the financial statements were available to be issued and determined there are no subsequent events that 
require disclosure other than those discussed in Note 11.

Note 3—Revenue and receivables 
RITI accounted for revenue under the provisions of ASC 606, Revenue from Contracts with Customers. Under 
ASC  606,  revenue  is  recognized  when  RITI  transfers  the  promised  goods  or  services  to  a  customer  in  an 
amount that reflects consideration that is expected to be received for those goods and services. 
Performance  Obligations  –  A  performance  obligation  is  a  promise  in  a  contract  to  transfer  a  distinct  good  or 
service  to  the  customer  and  is  the  unit  of  account  under  ASC  606.  The  transaction  price  is  allocated  to  each 
distinct  performance  obligation  and  is  recognized  as  revenue  when,  or  as,  each  performance  obligation  is 
satisfied. RITI’s primary revenue streams do not fall within the scope of ASC 606.

Note 4—Fair value measurement of investments 
RITI has adopted the provisions of the Fair Value Measurement topic of FASB ASC. This guidance establishes 
a framework for measuring fair value of financial assets and financial liabilities. That framework provides a fair 
value  hierarchy  that  prioritizes  the  inputs  to  valuation  techniques  used  to  measure  fair  value.  The  hierarchy 
gives  the  highest  priority  to  unadjusted  quoted  prices  in  active  markets  for  identical  assets  or  liabilities 
(Level 1 measurements)  and  the  lowest  priority  to  unobservable  inputs  (Level  3  measurements).  The  three 
levels of the fair value hierarchy are described below: 
Level 1 – Inputs to the valuation methodology are unadjusted quoted prices for identical assets or liabilities 
in active markets that RITI has the ability to access. 
Level 2 – Inputs to the valuation methodology include: 
  Quoted prices for similar assets or liabilities in active markets; 
  Quoted prices for identical or similar assets or liabilities in inactive markets;

Inputs  that  are  derived  principally  from  or  corroborated  by  the  observable  market  data  by

If  the  asset  or  liability  has  a  specified  (contractual)  term,  the  Level  2  input  must  be  observable  for

Note 6—Paycheck Protection Program loan 
In 2020, RITI received a Paycheck Protection Program (“PPP”) loan in the amount of $425,000. The PPP loan 
was  granted  by  the  Small  Business  Administration  under  the  Coronavirus  Aid,  Relief,  and  Economic  Security 
Act  (“CARES  Act”).  PPP  loans  are  considered  conditional  contributions  under  ASC  958-605,  Not-for-Profit 
Entities – Revenue Recognition. The PPP loan must be repaid if RITI does not overcome certain barriers within 
the  CARES  Act.  The  barriers  under  the  program  include  the  requirement  to  maintain  employee  headcount, 
spend  up  to  60%  of  the  loan  proceeds  on  certain  payroll  and  employee  benefits,  and  restricts  other  loan 
proceeds to be used for other qualifying expenses such as mortgage interest, rent, and utilities. During 2021, 
RITI  completed  the  forgiveness  application  process  upon  completion  of  the  applicable  24-week  period  and 
received  notice  on  November  5,  2020  that  the  PPP  loan  has  been  forgiven.  RITI  reflected  the  original  loan 
amount as loan forgiveness revenue on the statement of activities for the year ended June 30, 2021.

recognized the ERC when the qualifying wages were incurred and any barriers to realization were overcome, 
which was deemed to be during the year ended June 30, 2022 with the filing of the amended payroll tax returns.

June  30,  2022  statement  of  financial  position  and  statement  of  activities  for  the  year  ended  June  30,  2022, 
respectively. 
Subsequent to June 30, 2022, the Organization received the ERC for the third and fourth quarters of 2020 in the 
amount  of  $41,093.  The  ERC  for  all  other  quarters  in  2020  and  2021  remains  outstanding  as  of  January  10,

Report of Independent Auditor
To the Board of Directors
Room In The Inn, Inc.
Nashville, Tennessee
Opinion
We have audited the accompanying financial statements of Room In The Inn, Inc. (a nonprofit organization) (the
“Organization”), which comprise the statements of financial position as of June 30, 2022 and 2021, and the
related statements of activities, functional expenses, and cash flows for the years then ended, and the related
notes to the financial statements.
In our opinion, the financial statements referred to above present fairly, in all material respects, the financial
position of the Organization as of June 30, 2022 and 2021, and the changes in its net assets and its cash flows
for the years then ended in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of
America.
Basis for Opinion
We conducted our audits in accordance with auditing standards generally accepted in the United States of
America. Our responsibilities under those standards are further described in the Auditor’s Responsibilities for
the Audit of the Financial Statements section of our report. We are required to be independent of the
organization and to meet our other ethical responsibilities in accordance with the relevant ethical requirements
relating to our audits. We believe the audit evidence we have obtained is sufficient and appropriate to provide a
basis for our audit opinion.
Responsibility of Management for the Financial Statements
Management is responsible for the preparation and fair presentation of these financial statements in accordance
with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America; this includes the design,
implementation, and maintenance of internal control relevant to the preparation and fair presentation of financial
statements that are free from material misstatement, whether due to fraud or error.
In preparing the financial statements, management is required to evaluate whether there are conditions or
events, considered in the aggregate, that raise substantial doubt about Organization’s ability to continue as a
going concern within one year after the date the financial statements are available to be issued.
Auditor’s Responsibilities for the Audit of the Financial Statements
Our objectives are to obtain reasonable assurance about whether the financial statements as a whole are free
from material misstatement, whether due to fraud or error, and to issue an auditor’s report that includes our
opinion. Reasonable assurance is a high level of assurance but is not absolute assurance and, therefore, is not
a guarantee that an audit conducted in accordance with generally accepted auditing standards will always
detect a material misstatement when it exists. The risk of not detecting a material misstatement resulting from
fraud is higher than for one resulting from error, as fraud may involve collusion, forgery, intentional omissions,
misrepresentations, or the override of internal control. Misstatements are considered material if there is a
substantial likelihood that, individually or in the aggregate, they would influence the judgment made by a
reasonable user based on the financial statements.

ROOM IN THE INN, INC.
NOTES TO THE FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
JUNE 30, 2022 AND 2021
Note 1—Nature of organization and significant accounting policies
Organization – Room In The Inn, Inc. (“RITI”) is a religious non-profit organization based in Nashville,
Tennessee. RITI is committed to providing enhanced services to the homeless while improving the system by
which these services are delivered. RITI administers a variety of programs to provide a continuum of care that is
emergency and long-term, residential, and educational. The following is a description of selected RITI programs.
The Day Center serves homeless individuals with daytime shelter and educational opportunities throughout the
year. The Guest House serves homeless substance abusers by offering shelter to individuals who are
undergoing alcohol and drug addiction treatment through a partnership with United Neighborhood Health and
the chronic homeless program through the Veterans’ Administration. It also provides transitional housing and
supportive services for homeless men from the general population. The Veterans program provides transitional
housing and supportive services to homeless veterans. The Permanent Housing program provides
income-based housing for up to 38 homeless participants. Respite offers homeless individuals who are
medically fragile a place to recover. Prior to the pandemic, RITI partnered with more than 180 Middle
Tennessee congregations and provided shelter for an average of 250 men, women, and children each evening
during the winter months. The pandemic cut the congregations and shelter beds almost in half, but the program
continues to rebuild each year.
Basis of Presentation – In accordance with Financial Accounting Standards Board (“FASB”) Accounting
Standards Codification (“ASC”) guidelines, RITI reports information regarding its financial position and activities
according to two classes of net assets based on the existence or absence of donor-imposed restrictions.
Accordingly, the net assets of RITI and changes therein are classified and reported as follows:
Net Assets Without Donor Restrictions – Net assets that are not subject to donor-imposed restrictions, and
may be expended for any purpose in performing the primary objectives of RITI. These net assets may be
used at the discretion of RITI’s management and Board of Directors.
Net Assets With Donor Restrictions – Net assets subject to stipulations imposed by donors and grantors.
Some donor restrictions are temporary in nature; those restrictions will be met by actions of RITI or by the
passage of time. Other donor restrictions are perpetual in nature, whereby the donor has stipulated the
funds be maintained in perpetuity. RITI held no net assets with donor restrictions at June 30, 2022 or 2021.
Cash and Cash Equivalents – For purposes of the statements of cash flows, RITI considers all unrestricted
highly liquid investments with an initial maturity of three months or less to be cash equivalents. The cash
accounts are held primarily by financial institutions and at times may exceed amounts that are federally insured.
Contributions Receivable – Contributions are recognized when the donor makes a promise to give to RITI that
is, in substance, unconditional. Contributions are recognized when received as contributions without restriction if
specified for the current period and there are no donor-imposed restrictions. Contributions specified for future
periods or with donor-imposed restrictions are recognized in the period received as contributions with
restrictions. Contributions that are restricted by the donor are reported as increases in net assets without
restrictions if the restrictions are satisfied in the year in which the contributions are recognized.
RITI uses the allowance method to determine uncollectible unconditional promises to give. The allowance is
based on prior years’ experience and management’s analysis of specific promises made.
Investments – RITI accounts for investments using FASB ASC guidance for investments by nonprofit organizations.
Under this guidance, investments in marketable securities with readily determinable fair values and other readily
marketable assets are valued at their fair values in the statements of financial position. Unrealized gains and losses
are included in the change in net assets. See Note 4 for additional information on fair value measurements.

NOTES TO THE FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
JUNE 30, 2022 AND 2021
Note 1—Nature of organization and significant accounting policies (continued)
Land, Building, and Equipment – RITI capitalizes all expenditures for land, building, and equipment in excess of
$1,000. Purchases of land, building, and equipment are carried at cost. Donated property and equipment are carried
at the approximate fair value at the date of donation. Depreciation is computed using the straight-line method over
estimated useful lives of 5 to 39 years.
Income Taxes – RITI is exempt from federal income taxes under Section 501(c)(3) of the Internal Revenue Code,
and is not a private foundation. Accordingly, no provision for income taxes has been made in the accompanying
financial statements.
RITI follows FASB ASC guidance related to unrecognized tax benefits. The guidance clarifies the accounting for
uncertainty in income taxes recognized in an organization’s financial statements. This guidance prescribes a
minimum probability threshold that a tax position must meet before a financial statement benefit is recognized. The
minimum threshold is defined as a tax position that is more likely than not to be sustained upon examination by the
applicable taxing authority, including resolution of any related appeals or litigation processes, based on the technical
merits of the position. The tax benefit to be recognized is measured as the largest amount of benefit that is greater
than 50% likely of being realized upon ultimate settlement. RITI has no tax penalties or interest reported in the
accompanying financial statements.
Use of Estimates – The preparation of financial statements in conformity with accounting principles generally
accepted in the United States of America (“U.S. GAAP”) requires management to make estimates and assumptions
that affect the reported amounts of assets and liabilities and disclosure of contingent assets and liabilities at the date
of the financial statements and the reported amounts of revenues and expenses during the reporting period. Actual
results could differ from those estimates.
Contributed Materials and Services – Contributed materials and equipment, if any, are reflected as contributed
nonfinancial assets in the accompanying financial statements at their estimated values at the date of receipt.
Contributed use of facilities is recorded at the estimated fair market value.
Contributions of donated services that create or enhance nonfinancial assets or that require specialized skills, are
provided by individuals possessing those skills, and would typically need to be purchased if not provided by
donation, are recorded at their fair values in the period received.
Additionally, a number of non-professional volunteers donated approximately 21,900 and 9,984 hours during the
years ended June 30, 2022 and 2021, respectively, to RITI’s program services. However, these services do not
meet the requirements above and have not been recorded.
Functional Allocation of Expenses – The costs of providing program and other activities have been summarized
on a functional basis in the statements of activities. While most costs have been directly assigned to a functional
category, certain joint costs have been allocated among program services and supporting services benefited.
Such allocations are determined by management on an equitable basis. Expenses that are allocated consist
primarily of salaries and wages expense which is allocated based on time and effort.

NOTES TO THE FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
JUNE 30, 2022 AND 2021
Note 1—Nature of organization and significant accounting policies (continued)
Recently Adopted Accounting Pronouncements – In September 2020, FASB issued Accounting Standards
Update (“ASU”) 2020-07, Presentation and Disclosures by Not-for-Profit Entities for Contributed Nonfinancial
Assets. This ASU requires not-for-profit entities to present contributed nonfinancial assets as a separate line
item in the statement of activities, apart from contributions of cash and other financial assets. In addition, for
each category of contributed nonfinancial assets recognized, certain additional disclosures are required. This
standard is effective for the year ending June 30, 2022. There have been no donor restrictions placed on such
contributions.
Accounting Policies for Future Pronouncements – In February 2016, FASB issued ASU 2016-02, Leases. The
standard requires all leases with lease terms over 12 months to be capitalized as a right-of-use asset and lease
liability on the statement of financial position at the date of lease commencement. Leases will be classified as
either finance or operating. This distinction will be relevant for the pattern of expense recognition in the
statement of activities. This standard will be effective for the fiscal year ending June 30, 2023. RITI is currently
evaluating the effect of the implementation of this new standard.
Subsequent Events – RITI has evaluated subsequent events and transactions through January 10, 2023, the
date the financial statements were available to be issued and determined there are no subsequent events that

RITI accounted for revenue under the provisions of ASC 606, Revenue from Contracts with Customers. Under
ASC 606, revenue is recognized when RITI transfers the promised goods or services to a customer in an
amount that reflects consideration that is expected to be received for those goods and services.
Performance Obligations – A performance obligation is a promise in a contract to transfer a distinct good or
service to the customer and is the unit of account under ASC 606. The transaction price is allocated to each
distinct performance obligation and is recognized as revenue when, or as, each performance obligation is
satisfied. RITI’s primary revenue streams do not fall within the scope of ASC 606.
Accounts Receivable – Accounts receivable relating to grants and pledges totaled $87,310 and $54,273 at
June 30, 2022 and 2021, respectively. Contributions receivable of $8,209 were written off for the year ended
June 30, 2022. There were no write-offs of contributions receivable for the year ended June 30, 2021.
Note 4—Fair value measurement of investments
RITI has adopted the provisions of the Fair Value Measurement topic of FASB ASC. This guidance establishes
a framework for measuring fair value of financial assets and financial liabilities. That framework provides a fair
value hierarchy that prioritizes the inputs to valuation techniques used to measure fair value. The hierarchy
gives the highest priority to unadjusted quoted prices in active markets for identical assets or liabilities
(Level 1 measurements) and the lowest priority to unobservable inputs (Level 3 measurements). The three
levels of the fair value hierarchy are described below:
Level 1 – Inputs to the valuation methodology are unadjusted quoted prices for identical assets or liabilities
in active markets that RITI has the ability to access.
Level 2 – Inputs to the valuation methodology include:
 Quoted prices for similar assets or liabilities in active markets;
 Quoted prices for identical or similar assets or liabilities in inactive markets;


Inputs other than quoted prices that are observable for the asset or liability; and
Inputs that are derived principally from or corroborated by the observable market data by
correlation or other means.
If the asset or liability has a specified (contractual) term, the Level 2 input must be observable for
substantially the full term of the asset or liability.
Level 3 – Inputs to the valuation methodology are unobservable and significant to the fair value
measurement.

Note 6—Paycheck Protection Program loan
In 2020, RITI received a Paycheck Protection Program (“PPP”) loan in the amount of $425,000. The PPP loan
was granted by the Small Business Administration under the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security
Act (“CARES Act”). PPP loans are considered conditional contributions under ASC 958-605, Not-for-Profit
Entities – Revenue Recognition. The PPP loan must be repaid if RITI does not overcome certain barriers within
the CARES Act. The barriers under the program include the requirement to maintain employee headcount,
spend up to 60% of the loan proceeds on certain payroll and employee benefits, and restricts other loan
proceeds to be used for other qualifying expenses such as mortgage interest, rent, and utilities. During 2021,
RITI completed the forgiveness application process upon completion of the applicable 24-week period and
received notice on November 5, 2020 that the PPP loan has been forgiven. RITI reflected the original loan
amount as loan forgiveness revenue on the statement of activities for the year ended June 30, 2021.

Note 10—Employee retirement plan

Note 11—Employee Retention Credit
The CARES Act contains the Employee Retention Credit (“ERC”), a refundable payroll tax credit available to
employers that have experienced hardship in their operations due to the COVID-19 outbreak. The Organization
qualified for $840,406 of ERC for various quarters during the years ended June 30, 2022 and 2021. The
Organization selected ASC 958-605 as the applicable standard for accounting for ERC and, as such,
recognized the ERC when the qualifying wages were incurred and any barriers to realization were overcome,
which was deemed to be during the year ended June 30, 2022 with the filing of the amended payroll tax returns.
$840,406 has been recorded as Employee Retention Credit receivable and Employee Retention Credit in the
June 30, 2022 statement of financial position and statement of activities for the year ended June 30, 2022,
respectively.
Subsequent to June 30, 2022, the Organization received the ERC for the third and fourth quarters of 2020 in the
amount of $41,093. The ERC for all other quarters in 2020 and 2021 remains outstanding as of January 10,
2023.

One city for all people 
6/30/26 
Davie Tucker, Jr. 
Executive Director    
TO:       
 Complainant 
, Complainant 
Commissioners  
Dahron Johnson, Chair  
Keri Adams 
Garlinda Burton  
Amy Crawford Charlton 
Erin Coleman  
Katie Feldhaus 
Dakota Galban  
Cara Ince  
Sarah Martin 
Todd McKinney  
Whitney Pastorek  
Carmen Reese Foster 
William Slone 
Jeff Teague  
Ben Tran 
, Complainant 
Office of Homeless Services, Respondent 
Derrick Smith, Attorney for Respondent 
Dahron Johnson, Chair of the Metro Human Relations Commission 
RE: Probable Cause Determination of January 23, 2026 Complaint 
This correspondence contains the probable cause determination of the Metro 
Nashville Human Relations Commission ("MHRC") regarding the notarized 
complaint received on January 23, 2026, against the Office of Homeless 
Services (“OHS”).  
First, we acknowledge and appreciate the time, documentation, and 
engagement that has been provided throughout this process, including 
participation in the formal complaint process and the supplemental 
information provided. We have carefully reviewed all submissions, including 
correspondence and supporting documentation in accordance with MHRC 
Rules and Procedures governing intake, investigation, and determination. I, in 
my capacity as MHRC’s Executive Director, hereby adopt the Staff Investigative 
Report’s Findings of Fact and incorporates them by reference as the factual 
basis for this Determination. 
Procedural Background 
Claudia Weber 
The record reflects the following relevant procedural history: 
Alecia Wynn 
•  August 28, 2025 – A Title VI inquiry was submitted to the Metro Human 
Relations Commission through HubNashville alleging discrmination of 
federally-funded housing assistance by the Office of Homeless 
Services. 
•  September 2, 2025 – MHRC staff contacted the complainant and 
scheduled an intake conference for September 5, 2025. 
•  September 5, 2025 - MHRC staff conducted an intake interview with the 
complainant regarding the allegations.  
•  October 17, 2025 - The complainant resigned from employment with 
Step Up and submitted a written statement to MHRC concerning the 
matters under investigation. 
•  October 22, 2025 - MHRC initiated its first informal outreach to OHS by 
contacting the OHS Program manager regarding the Title VI inquiry. The
One city for all people 
Program Manager referred MHRC to the OHS Public Information Officer 
(PIO). The PIO advised that she would respond in 2 days. 
•  October 24, 2025 – The OHS Public Information Officer informed MHRC 
that the inquiry had been forwarded to the Department of Legal for 
guidance. 
•  October 27, 2025 – The OHS Public Information Officer responded that 
OHS had been advised the matter was not a Title VI issue and stated 
that the individuals referenced in inquiry were no longer eligible for 
assistance because they were “no longer homeless.” 
•  October 28, 2025 – MHRC contacted the OHS Public Information 
Officer, the Department of Law, and the Director of OHS requesting an 
informal meeting to discuss resolution of the Title VI concerns prior to 
the filling of a formal complaint. 
•  October 31, 2025 – An OHS Administrative Services Manager requested 
additional information regarding the allegations but did not respond to 
MHRC’s requst for an informal meeting. 
•  December 9, 2025 – MHRC provided additional information regarding 
the allegations and again requsted a meeting with OHS in an effort to 
resolve the matter informally.   
January 23, 2026 – Following unsuccessful informal efforts, a formal 
Title VI complaint was filed with MHRC. 
• 
•  February 4, 2026 – After determining that the complaint falls within the 
jurisdiction of the Commission and that the complaint alleges 
circumstances that warrant an investigation into whether 
discrimination or a discrimination practice occurred, the Executive 
Director served the formal complaint to OHS and requested a written 
response by March 6, 2026 
•  March 4, 2026 – MHRC and counsel from the Department of Law 
reached an agreement in principle to temporarily suspend the 
investigative response deadline while the parties pursued an informal 
pre-conciliation process.   
•  March 11, 2026 – MHRC requested confirmation from OHS regarding

Under MHRC Rules and Procedures, a finding of probable cause requires 
sufficient evidence to support a reasonable belief that unlawful discrimination 
has occurred. The MHRC is required to evaluate whether the evidence 
establishes a nexus between the alleged conduct and a protected class under 
Title VI, and whether the conduct rises to the level of a violation within the 
Commission's jurisdiction.

2.  OHS selected eight participants from the Nashville Rescue Mission;

this population.

must be taken to eliminate the alleged   discriminatory practice.

Staff Investigative Report 
June 26, 2026 
I. Introduction 
This report presents the findings of the Metropolitan Human Relations Commission ("MHRC") 
staff following an investigation into allegations concerning the administration of federally-
funded housing assistance and housing stabilization services by the Metropolitan Government of 
Nashville and Davidson County Office of Homeless Services ("OHS"). The investigation was 
conducted pursuant to the Commission's authority under the Metropolitan Charter, the 
Metropolitan Code of Laws, the Commission's Rules and Procedures, and applicable federal civil 
rights laws governing recipients of federal financial assistance. 
The investigation concerns allegations that OHS, in administering bridge housing placements, 
rental assistance, housing navigation services, and access to permanent housing resources, may 
have employed inconsistent or inadequately-defined policies and practices that resulted in 
unequal treatment or a disparate impact on protected classes, particularly Black women and 
women of color experiencing homelessness. 
The allegations arise from complaints submitted to the Commission, documentary evidence 
obtained during the investigation, interviews with complainants, current and former service 
providers, former OHS personnel, and other witnesses possessing relevant information regarding 
the administration of these programs. 
The purpose of this report is not to determine ultimate liability or make findings equivalent to 
those rendered by a court of law. Rather, consistent with Rule 2.7 of the MHRC Rules and 
Procedures, this report evaluates whether sufficient evidence exists to establish probable cause to 
believe that an unlawful discriminatory practice may have occurred, thereby warranting further 
proceedings, including conciliation. 
II. Jurisdiction 
The Metropolitan Human Relations Commission is authorized to investigate allegations of 
unlawful discrimination within its jurisdiction, including discrimination arising from the 
administration of federally-assisted programs and activities. 
At all times relevant to this investigation, the Office of Homeless Services administered or 
coordinated programs supported through federal financial assistance, including funding 
authorized under the American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA), U.S. Department of Housing and 
Urban Development (HUD) programs, Continuum of Care (CoC) funding, Emergency Solutions 
Grant (ESG) funding, and other federal and local housing initiatives. OHS exercised substantial 
authority over participant selection, housing placement, funding allocation, housing navigation, 
rental assistance administration, and coordination with nonprofit service providers participating 
in federally-funded homelessness response systems. 
1
Because these programs were administered with federal financial assistance, they are subject to 
the nondiscrimination requirements of Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and its 
implementing regulations, which prohibit discrimination on the basis of race, color, or national 
origin in programs receiving federal financial assistance, as well as state and local law and 
policy. 
Accordingly, MHRC possesses jurisdiction to investigate whether the administration of these 
federally assisted housing programs complied with applicable civil rights requirements. 
III. Scope of Investigation 
The investigation examined the administration of bridge housing and related housing 
stabilization initiatives occurring approximately between August 2024 and September 2025, 
including, but not limited to: 
rental assistance commitments; 
access to permanent housing resources; 
•  participant identification and selection; 
•  vulnerability assessments and prioritization methodologies; 
•  housing navigation services; 
• 
•  bridge housing placements; 
• 
•  housing voucher referrals; 
•  participant exits; 
•  modification or termination of rental assistance; 
•  program oversight and decision-making; 
• 
• 
communications with contracted service providers; and 
implementation of policies governing these activities. 
The investigation also examined whether OHS maintained objective standards governing these 
decisions and whether such standards were applied consistently across similarly situated 
participants. 
Although the investigation includes the experiences of individual complainants and witnesses, 
the inquiry is not limited to the circumstances of any single participant. Rather, the investigation 
evaluates whether the design or administration of the relevant programs resulted in systemic 
inequities affecting participants receiving federally funded housing services. 
IV. Allegations 
The investigation was conducted to determine whether the evidence supports the following 
findings: 
1. Whether OHS administered federally funded housing programs pursuant to written policies, 
objective eligibility criteria, and consistently applied procedures governing participant selection, 
rental assistance, and housing transitions. 
2
2. Whether participants for bridge housing, rental assistance, and housing navigation services 
were selected using transparent, documented, and consistently applied criteria, including whether 
Coordinated Entry tools or standardized prioritization systems were uniformly utilized. 
3. Whether participants received accurate, consistent, and complete information regarding 
duration of rental assistance, eligibility for housing vouchers, and pathways to permanent 
housing. 
4. Whether modifications to rental assistance or participant financial obligations were 
implemented pursuant to established policies, and whether such changes were consistently 
communicated and documented. 
5. Whether OHS maintained adequate documentation supporting participant selection, 
prioritization decisions, voucher referrals, program exits, and rental assistance determinations. 
6. Whether similarly-situated participants received different treatment with respect to housing 
placement, rental assistance, voucher access, or program continuation without documented 
justification. 
7. Whether facially-neutral policies or practices governing shelter exits, housing placement, and 
rental assistance had a disproportionate adverse impact on protected classes, including Black 
women and women of color experiencing homelessness. 
8. Whether the totality of the evidence supports a reasonable basis to believe that the 
administration of federally funded housing programs by OHS may have violated Title VI or 
related nondiscrimination requirements. 
V. Standard of Review 
Pursuant to Rule 2.7 of the MHRC Rules and Procedures, the purpose of an investigation is to 
determine whether probable cause exists to believe that an unlawful discriminatory practice may 
have occurred. 
Probable cause is a threshold determination. It does not require proof by a preponderance of the 
evidence or proof beyond a reasonable doubt. Rather, the inquiry is whether the evidence, 
viewed as a whole, provides a reasonable basis to believe that unlawful discrimination may have 
occurred and that further proceedings are warranted. 
Where evidence was conflicting, staff evaluated credibility based upon corroboration, 
consistency, documentary support, contemporaneous records, and the plausibility of each 
account when considered in context of the entire investigative record. 
No adverse inference was drawn solely from disputed testimony where documentary evidence 
remained incomplete or unavailable. 
VI. Documents Reviewed and Witnesses Interviewed 
3
The investigation included review of documentary records, communications, policies, contracts, 
and funding materials obtained from the parties and third parties, as well as interviews with 
complainants, current and former employees of participating organizations, and former OHS 
personnel, housing providers, and other individuals possessing relevant knowledge. 
Investigators also examined publicly available information concerning the operation of 
Nashville's homelessness response system, Continuum of Care requirements, HUD guidance, 
applicable grant requirements, and demographic information relevant to the administration of 
homeless services. 
Where appropriate, investigative findings were evaluated against nationally recognized 
principles governing equitable administration of federally funded programs and the requirements 
of Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. 
VIII. Background Information 
The Office of Homeless Services ("OHS") serves as Metropolitan Nashville and Davidson 
County's lead agency for coordinating the local response to homelessness. During the period 
relevant to this investigation, OHS administered, coordinated, or oversaw numerous housing and 
homelessness initiatives funded through a combination of federal, state, local, and private 
resources. 
Among its responsibilities, OHS coordinated emergency shelter operations, housing navigation, 
landlord engagement, rental assistance, supportive services, homeless management information 
systems, and the administration of federal grants intended to increase access to stable housing for 
individuals and families experiencing homelessness. 
OHS also served as a central coordinating entity among nonprofit service providers, property 
owners, housing developers, and governmental partners participating in Nashville's homelessness 
response system. 
Because many of these activities were supported through federal financial assistance, OHS was 
required to administer its programs in accordance with applicable federal civil rights 
requirements, including Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. 
Nashville participates in HUD's Continuum of Care ("CoC") program, which is intended to 
create a coordinated system for addressing homelessness through community-wide planning, 
prioritization, and allocation of housing resources. 
As part of the CoC framework, participating agencies utilize a Coordinated Entry process 
designed to assess individuals and families experiencing homelessness, evaluate vulnerability 
and housing needs, and prioritize participants for available housing resources. 
The Coordinated Entry system is intended to promote consistency, transparency, and equitable 
access by reducing reliance upon informal referrals or subjective decision-making. Under this 
framework, participants are generally assessed using standardized tools and referred to available 
4
housing resources according to established prioritization criteria, while recognizing that certain 
funding streams or specialized programs may have additional eligibility requirements. 
The effectiveness of Coordinated Entry depends upon the consistent application of objective 
criteria and accurate documentation of participant assessments, referrals, and program status1. 
The demographic composition of the population served by Nashville's homelessness response 
system provides important context for evaluating the potential impact of administrative 
decisions. 
Nationally, Black individuals and families are disproportionately represented among people 
experiencing homelessness despite comprising a substantially smaller percentage of the overall 
population2. Research has consistently shown that Black families, particularly Black women with 
children, are overrepresented among households utilizing emergency shelters and family shelter 
systems3. 
Available national outreach data and point-in-time count similarly indicate that families residing 
in Nashville's emergency shelters include a disproportionately high percentage of Black residents 
and other people of color4. By contrast, outreach data and point-in-time counts have often shown 
a comparatively higher proportion of unsheltered individuals living in encampments who 
identify as White, although demographic patterns vary over time and by location. 
These demographic realities do not establish discrimination. They do, however, underscore why 
decisions affecting access to shelter exits, bridge housing, rental assistance, and permanent 
housing opportunities warrant careful examination under Title VI when the affected participant 
population is disproportionately composed of members of protected classes. 
IX. Factual Findings 
1. The Office of Homeless Services (OHS) administered and/or coordinated federally funded 
housing and homelessness response programs during the period August 2024 through August 
2025, including programs supported by ARPA and related funding streams.  
2. OHS partnered with nonprofit service providers, including Step Up and others, to implement 
housing placement, rental assistance, and housing navigation services. 
1 See guidance from the US Department of Housing and Urban Development: https://endhomelessness.org/wp-
content/uploads/2024/10/Coordinated-Entry-Core-Elements.pdf 
2 Fusaro V.A., Levy H.G., Shaefer H.L. Racial and ethnic disparities in the lifetime prevalence of homelessness in the 
United States. Demography. 2018;55(6) 
3 Willison, Charley et al. “Persistent Disparities: Trends in Rates of Sheltered Homelessness Across Demographic 
Subgroups in the USA.” Journal of Racial and Ethnic Health Disparities vol. 11,1 (2024): 326-338. 
4 See https://files.hudexchange.info/reports/published/CoC_PopSub_NatlTerrDC_2025.pdf, 
https://endhomelessness.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/DDP-Race-brief-09272019-byline-single-pages-2.pdf 
5
3. Participants in the program at issue were primarily individuals and families experiencing 
homelessness who had previously been residing in emergency shelter, namely the Nashville 
Rescue Mission.  
4. Participants were placed into apartment units at properties including The Ave and Hillside 
Crossing under arrangements involving OHS, service providers, and property managers. 
5. The initiative involved a combination of housing placement, rental assistance, and supportive 
services intended to stabilize participants and transition them toward permanent housing.  
6. Eight families were selected for placement at The Ave and Hillside Crossing from emergency 
shelter populations, including individuals experiencing “overflow” conditions at the Nashville 
Rescue Mission.  
7. Witness testimony indicates that participants were informed they were being moved into 
housing with supportive services intended to facilitate long-term stability.  
8. The investigation has not yet obtained complete documentation demonstrating the specific 
criteria used to select individual participants for placement in the initiative. (OHS has not 
responded to requests regarding this finding) 
9. The record contains conflicting accounts regarding whether standardized Coordinated Entry 
prioritization tools were used to select all participants for placement.  
10. Witnesses report that OHS or its partners initially represented that rental assistance would be 
provided for a defined period, including references to approximately one year of rent support in 
certain cases. 
11. Participants later experienced reductions in rental assistance obligations, including transitions 
toward increased tenant responsibility for rent payments.  
12. Multiple witnesses reported that, during late 2024 through 2025, OHS and/or partner 
agencies discussed changes to rental assistance structure due to funding constraints.  
13. Witness testimony describes the development of a phased rent reduction or “breakdown 
plan” under which participant rent obligations increased over time while program subsidies 
decreased.  
14. Participants were subsequently notified of increased rent obligations during 2025.  
15. Several participants reported receiving lease violation notices, eviction notices, or rent 
demands following reductions in rental assistance.  
16. Participants described the changes in rent obligations as destabilizing and inconsistent with 
their understanding of the terms under which they entered the program. 
6
17. Two of the eight participants did not obtain housing vouchers.  
18. The investigation has not yet received complete documentation identifying the written 
policies governing participant selection, rental assistance duration, or program exit criteria for 
the initiative.  
19. Multiple witnesses described variations in how policies were communicated and applied 
across participants and providers.  
20. The record reflects gaps in documentation regarding how individual participant decisions 
were made, including selection and prioritization decisions.  
21. A former Step Up employee reported concerns regarding changes in program administration, 
including rental assistance practices and participant treatment.  
22. The same witness reported being asked to revise a written statement and declining to do so 
based on professional ethics.  
23. The witness subsequently resigned from employment with Step Up.  
24. Witnesses reported internal communications emphasizing alignment or “unity” with OHS 
leadership in the context of provider advocacy concerns. 
25. Participants affected by the program at issue include a substantial proportion of Black 
women and women of color, consistent with demographic patterns of families experiencing 
sheltered homelessness in Nashville. 5 
26. National research indicates that Black households, particularly Black women with children, 
are disproportionately represented in sheltered homelessness populations compared to their share 
of the general population.6 
X. Findings on Allegations and Probable Cause Determination 
Based on the Findings of Fact set forth in Section IX, MHRC staff makes the following 
determinations as to each allegation: 
1.  Whether OHS administered federally-funded housing programs pursuant to written 
policies, objective eligibility criteria, and consistently applied procedures governing 
participant selection, rental assistance, and housing transitions. 
5 Six of the eight women participants, or 75%, identify as Black. 
6 See The 2025 Annual Homelessness Assessment Report (AHAR) to Congress: 
https://www.huduser.gov/portal/sites/default/files/pdf/2025-AHAR-Part-1.pdf 
7
The investigation finds that OHS has not produced complete written policies governing 
participant selection, rental assistance duration, or housing transition criteria for the initiative at 
issue.   
2.  Whether participants for bridge housing, rental assistance, and housing navigation 
services were selected using transparent, documented, and consistently applied criteria, 
including whether Coordinated Entry tools or standardized prioritization systems were 
uniformly utilized. 
The investigation finds that participants were selected from emergency shelter populations, 
including overflow populations from the Nashville Rescue Mission.  The record does not 
establish that standardized Coordinated Entry tools or documented prioritization criteria were 
uniformly applied to all participants. 
3.  Whether participants received accurate, consistent, and complete information regarding: 
duration of rental assistance, eligibility for housing vouchers, and pathways to 
permanent housing. 
The investigation finds the conflicting accounts regarding the information provided to 
participants concerning. 
4.  Whether modifications to rental assistance or participant financial obligations were 
implemented pursuant to established policies, and whether such changes were 
consistently communicated and documented. 
The investigation finds that participants experienced reductions in rental assistance obligations 
and/or increases in tenant responsibility during 2025. Witness testimony indicates these changes 
may have been implemented in response to funding concerns and were not consistently 
communicated across all participants. 
5.  Whether OHS maintained adequate documentation supporting: participant selection, 
prioritization decisions, voucher referrals, program exits, and rental assistance 
determinations. 
The investigation finds that OHS has failed to produce any written documentation nor responded 
to the multiple attempts to obtain answers to these questions. 
6.  Whether similarly situated participants received different treatment with respect to 
housing placement, rental assistance, voucher access, or program continuation without 
documented justification. 
The investigation finds that similarly situated participants experienced different outcomes with 
respect to rental assistance adjustments and housing transition outcomes. 
8
7.  Whether facially neutral policies or practices governing shelter exits, housing placement, 
and rental assistance had a disproportionate adverse impact on protected classes, 
including Black women and women of color experiencing homelessness. 
The investigation finds that the affected population includes a substantial proportion of Black 
women and women of color, shelter-based housing interventions disproportionately affect these 
populations nationally; and the challenged practices govern access to shelter exits, housing 
stability, and the 8 women and their children affected by OHS’s practices were 
disproportionately Black and women of color.  
8.  Whether the totality of the evidence supports a reasonable basis to believe that the 
administration of federally funded housing programs by OHS may have violated Title VI 
or related nondiscrimination requirements. 
Based on the totality of the evidence, the investigation finds that there is a probable cause to 
believe that OHS’s administration of federally-funded housing programs did not comply with 
Title VI requirements. 
9

This report presents the findings of the Metropolitan Human Relations Commission ("MHRC")
staff following an investigation into allegations concerning the administration of federally-
funded housing assistance and housing stabilization services by the Metropolitan Government of
Nashville and Davidson County Office of Homeless Services ("OHS"). The investigation was
conducted pursuant to the Commission's authority under the Metropolitan Charter, the
Metropolitan Code of Laws, the Commission's Rules and Procedures, and applicable federal civil
rights laws governing recipients of federal financial assistance.
The investigation concerns allegations that OHS, in administering bridge housing placements,
rental assistance, housing navigation services, and access to permanent housing resources, may
have employed inconsistent or inadequately-defined policies and practices that resulted in
unequal treatment or a disparate impact on protected classes, particularly Black women and
women of color experiencing homelessness.
The allegations arise from complaints submitted to the Commission, documentary evidence
obtained during the investigation, interviews with complainants, current and former service
providers, former OHS personnel, and other witnesses possessing relevant information regarding
the administration of these programs.
The purpose of this report is not to determine ultimate liability or make findings equivalent to
those rendered by a court of law. Rather, consistent with Rule 2.7 of the MHRC Rules and
Procedures, this report evaluates whether sufficient evidence exists to establish probable cause to
believe that an unlawful discriminatory practice may have occurred, thereby warranting further
proceedings, including conciliation.
II. Jurisdiction
The Metropolitan Human Relations Commission is authorized to investigate allegations of
unlawful discrimination within its jurisdiction, including discrimination arising from the
administration of federally-assisted programs and activities.
At all times relevant to this investigation, the Office of Homeless Services administered or
coordinated programs supported through federal financial assistance, including funding
authorized under the American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA), U.S. Department of Housing and
Urban Development (HUD) programs, Continuum of Care (CoC) funding, Emergency Solutions
Grant (ESG) funding, and other federal and local housing initiatives. OHS exercised substantial
authority over participant selection, housing placement, funding allocation, housing navigation,
rental assistance administration, and coordination with nonprofit service providers participating
in federally-funded homelessness response systems.
1

Because these programs were administered with federal financial assistance, they are subject to
the nondiscrimination requirements of Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and its
implementing regulations, which prohibit discrimination on the basis of race, color, or national
origin in programs receiving federal financial assistance, as well as state and local law and
policy.
Accordingly, MHRC possesses jurisdiction to investigate whether the administration of these
federally assisted housing programs complied with applicable civil rights requirements.
III. Scope of Investigation
The investigation examined the administration of bridge housing and related housing
stabilization initiatives occurring approximately between August 2024 and September 2025,
including, but not limited to:
rental assistance commitments;
access to permanent housing resources;
• participant identification and selection;
• vulnerability assessments and prioritization methodologies;
• housing navigation services;
•
• bridge housing placements;
•
• housing voucher referrals;
• participant exits;
• modification or termination of rental assistance;
• program oversight and decision-making;
•
•
communications with contracted service providers; and
implementation of policies governing these activities.
The investigation also examined whether OHS maintained objective standards governing these
decisions and whether such standards were applied consistently across similarly situated
participants.
Although the investigation includes the experiences of individual complainants and witnesses,
the inquiry is not limited to the circumstances of any single participant. Rather, the investigation
evaluates whether the design or administration of the relevant programs resulted in systemic
inequities affecting participants receiving federally funded housing services.
IV. Allegations
The investigation was conducted to determine whether the evidence supports the following
findings:
1. Whether OHS administered federally funded housing programs pursuant to written policies,
objective eligibility criteria, and consistently applied procedures governing participant selection,
rental assistance, and housing transitions.
2

2. Whether participants for bridge housing, rental assistance, and housing navigation services
were selected using transparent, documented, and consistently applied criteria, including whether
Coordinated Entry tools or standardized prioritization systems were uniformly utilized.
3. Whether participants received accurate, consistent, and complete information regarding
duration of rental assistance, eligibility for housing vouchers, and pathways to permanent
housing.
4. Whether modifications to rental assistance or participant financial obligations were
implemented pursuant to established policies, and whether such changes were consistently
communicated and documented.
5. Whether OHS maintained adequate documentation supporting participant selection,
prioritization decisions, voucher referrals, program exits, and rental assistance determinations.
6. Whether similarly-situated participants received different treatment with respect to housing
placement, rental assistance, voucher access, or program continuation without documented
justification.
7. Whether facially-neutral policies or practices governing shelter exits, housing placement, and
rental assistance had a disproportionate adverse impact on protected classes, including Black
women and women of color experiencing homelessness.
8. Whether the totality of the evidence supports a reasonable basis to believe that the
administration of federally funded housing programs by OHS may have violated Title VI or
related nondiscrimination requirements.
V. Standard of Review
Pursuant to Rule 2.7 of the MHRC Rules and Procedures, the purpose of an investigation is to
determine whether probable cause exists to believe that an unlawful discriminatory practice may
have occurred.
Probable cause is a threshold determination. It does not require proof by a preponderance of the
evidence or proof beyond a reasonable doubt. Rather, the inquiry is whether the evidence,
viewed as a whole, provides a reasonable basis to believe that unlawful discrimination may have
occurred and that further proceedings are warranted.
Where evidence was conflicting, staff evaluated credibility based upon corroboration,
consistency, documentary support, contemporaneous records, and the plausibility of each
account when considered in context of the entire investigative record.
No adverse inference was drawn solely from disputed testimony where documentary evidence
remained incomplete or unavailable.
VI. Documents Reviewed and Witnesses Interviewed
3

The investigation included review of documentary records, communications, policies, contracts,
and funding materials obtained from the parties and third parties, as well as interviews with
complainants, current and former employees of participating organizations, and former OHS
personnel, housing providers, and other individuals possessing relevant knowledge.
Investigators also examined publicly available information concerning the operation of
Nashville's homelessness response system, Continuum of Care requirements, HUD guidance,
applicable grant requirements, and demographic information relevant to the administration of
homeless services.
Where appropriate, investigative findings were evaluated against nationally recognized
principles governing equitable administration of federally funded programs and the requirements
of Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
VIII. Background Information
The Office of Homeless Services ("OHS") serves as Metropolitan Nashville and Davidson
County's lead agency for coordinating the local response to homelessness. During the period
relevant to this investigation, OHS administered, coordinated, or oversaw numerous housing and
homelessness initiatives funded through a combination of federal, state, local, and private
resources.
Among its responsibilities, OHS coordinated emergency shelter operations, housing navigation,
landlord engagement, rental assistance, supportive services, homeless management information
systems, and the administration of federal grants intended to increase access to stable housing for
individuals and families experiencing homelessness.
OHS also served as a central coordinating entity among nonprofit service providers, property
owners, housing developers, and governmental partners participating in Nashville's homelessness
response system.
Because many of these activities were supported through federal financial assistance, OHS was
required to administer its programs in accordance with applicable federal civil rights
requirements, including Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
Nashville participates in HUD's Continuum of Care ("CoC") program, which is intended to
create a coordinated system for addressing homelessness through community-wide planning,
prioritization, and allocation of housing resources.
As part of the CoC framework, participating agencies utilize a Coordinated Entry process
designed to assess individuals and families experiencing homelessness, evaluate vulnerability
and housing needs, and prioritize participants for available housing resources.
The Coordinated Entry system is intended to promote consistency, transparency, and equitable
access by reducing reliance upon informal referrals or subjective decision-making. Under this
framework, participants are generally assessed using standardized tools and referred to available
4

housing resources according to established prioritization criteria, while recognizing that certain
funding streams or specialized programs may have additional eligibility requirements.
The effectiveness of Coordinated Entry depends upon the consistent application of objective
criteria and accurate documentation of participant assessments, referrals, and program status1.
The demographic composition of the population served by Nashville's homelessness response
system provides important context for evaluating the potential impact of administrative
decisions.
Nationally, Black individuals and families are disproportionately represented among people
experiencing homelessness despite comprising a substantially smaller percentage of the overall
population2. Research has consistently shown that Black families, particularly Black women with
children, are overrepresented among households utilizing emergency shelters and family shelter
systems3.
Available national outreach data and point-in-time count similarly indicate that families residing
in Nashville's emergency shelters include a disproportionately high percentage of Black residents
and other people of color4. By contrast, outreach data and point-in-time counts have often shown
a comparatively higher proportion of unsheltered individuals living in encampments who
identify as White, although demographic patterns vary over time and by location.
These demographic realities do not establish discrimination. They do, however, underscore why
decisions affecting access to shelter exits, bridge housing, rental assistance, and permanent
housing opportunities warrant careful examination under Title VI when the affected participant
population is disproportionately composed of members of protected classes.
IX. Factual Findings
1. The Office of Homeless Services (OHS) administered and/or coordinated federally funded
housing and homelessness response programs during the period August 2024 through August
2025, including programs supported by ARPA and related funding streams.
2. OHS partnered with nonprofit service providers, including Step Up and others, to implement
housing placement, rental assistance, and housing navigation services.
1 See guidance from the US Department of Housing and Urban Development: https://endhomelessness.org/wp-
content/uploads/2024/10/Coordinated-Entry-Core-Elements.pdf
2 Fusaro V.A., Levy H.G., Shaefer H.L. Racial and ethnic disparities in the lifetime prevalence of homelessness in the
United States. Demography. 2018;55(6)
3 Willison, Charley et al. “Persistent Disparities: Trends in Rates of Sheltered Homelessness Across Demographic
Subgroups in the USA.” Journal of Racial and Ethnic Health Disparities vol. 11,1 (2024): 326-338.
4 See https://files.hudexchange.info/reports/published/CoC_PopSub_NatlTerrDC_2025.pdf,
https://endhomelessness.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/DDP-Race-brief-09272019-byline-single-pages-2.pdf
5

3. Participants in the program at issue were primarily individuals and families experiencing
homelessness who had previously been residing in emergency shelter, namely the Nashville
Rescue Mission.
4. Participants were placed into apartment units at properties including The Ave and Hillside
Crossing under arrangements involving OHS, service providers, and property managers.
5. The initiative involved a combination of housing placement, rental assistance, and supportive
services intended to stabilize participants and transition them toward permanent housing.
6. Eight families were selected for placement at The Ave and Hillside Crossing from emergency
shelter populations, including individuals experiencing “overflow” conditions at the Nashville
Rescue Mission.
7. Witness testimony indicates that participants were informed they were being moved into
housing with supportive services intended to facilitate long-term stability.
8. The investigation has not yet obtained complete documentation demonstrating the specific
criteria used to select individual participants for placement in the initiative. (OHS has not
responded to requests regarding this finding)
9. The record contains conflicting accounts regarding whether standardized Coordinated Entry
prioritization tools were used to select all participants for placement.
10. Witnesses report that OHS or its partners initially represented that rental assistance would be
provided for a defined period, including references to approximately one year of rent support in
certain cases.
11. Participants later experienced reductions in rental assistance obligations, including transitions
toward increased tenant responsibility for rent payments.
12. Multiple witnesses reported that, during late 2024 through 2025, OHS and/or partner
agencies discussed changes to rental assistance structure due to funding constraints.
13. Witness testimony describes the development of a phased rent reduction or “breakdown
plan” under which participant rent obligations increased over time while program subsidies
decreased.
14. Participants were subsequently notified of increased rent obligations during 2025.
15. Several participants reported receiving lease violation notices, eviction notices, or rent
demands following reductions in rental assistance.
16. Participants described the changes in rent obligations as destabilizing and inconsistent with
their understanding of the terms under which they entered the program.
6

17. Two of the eight participants did not obtain housing vouchers.
18. The investigation has not yet received complete documentation identifying the written
policies governing participant selection, rental assistance duration, or program exit criteria for
the initiative.
19. Multiple witnesses described variations in how policies were communicated and applied
across participants and providers.
20. The record reflects gaps in documentation regarding how individual participant decisions
were made, including selection and prioritization decisions.
21. A former Step Up employee reported concerns regarding changes in program administration,
including rental assistance practices and participant treatment.
22. The same witness reported being asked to revise a written statement and declining to do so
based on professional ethics.
23. The witness subsequently resigned from employment with Step Up.
24. Witnesses reported internal communications emphasizing alignment or “unity” with OHS
leadership in the context of provider advocacy concerns.
25. Participants affected by the program at issue include a substantial proportion of Black
women and women of color, consistent with demographic patterns of families experiencing
sheltered homelessness in Nashville. 5
26. National research indicates that Black households, particularly Black women with children,
are disproportionately represented in sheltered homelessness populations compared to their share
of the general population.6
X. Findings on Allegations and Probable Cause Determination
Based on the Findings of Fact set forth in Section IX, MHRC staff makes the following
determinations as to each allegation:
1. Whether OHS administered federally-funded housing programs pursuant to written
policies, objective eligibility criteria, and consistently applied procedures governing
participant selection, rental assistance, and housing transitions.
5 Six of the eight women participants, or 75%, identify as Black.
6 See The 2025 Annual Homelessness Assessment Report (AHAR) to Congress:
https://www.huduser.gov/portal/sites/default/files/pdf/2025-AHAR-Part-1.pdf
7

The investigation finds that OHS has not produced complete written policies governing
participant selection, rental assistance duration, or housing transition criteria for the initiative at
issue.
2. Whether participants for bridge housing, rental assistance, and housing navigation
services were selected using transparent, documented, and consistently applied criteria,
including whether Coordinated Entry tools or standardized prioritization systems were
uniformly utilized.
The investigation finds that participants were selected from emergency shelter populations,
including overflow populations from the Nashville Rescue Mission. The record does not
establish that standardized Coordinated Entry tools or documented prioritization criteria were
uniformly applied to all participants.
3. Whether participants received accurate, consistent, and complete information regarding:
duration of rental assistance, eligibility for housing vouchers, and pathways to
permanent housing.
The investigation finds the conflicting accounts regarding the information provided to
participants concerning.
4. Whether modifications to rental assistance or participant financial obligations were
implemented pursuant to established policies, and whether such changes were
consistently communicated and documented.
The investigation finds that participants experienced reductions in rental assistance obligations
and/or increases in tenant responsibility during 2025. Witness testimony indicates these changes
may have been implemented in response to funding concerns and were not consistently
communicated across all participants.
5. Whether OHS maintained adequate documentation supporting: participant selection,
prioritization decisions, voucher referrals, program exits, and rental assistance
determinations.
The investigation finds that OHS has failed to produce any written documentation nor responded
to the multiple attempts to obtain answers to these questions.
6. Whether similarly situated participants received different treatment with respect to
housing placement, rental assistance, voucher access, or program continuation without
documented justification.
The investigation finds that similarly situated participants experienced different outcomes with
respect to rental assistance adjustments and housing transition outcomes.
8

7. Whether facially neutral policies or practices governing shelter exits, housing placement,
and rental assistance had a disproportionate adverse impact on protected classes,
including Black women and women of color experiencing homelessness.
The investigation finds that the affected population includes a substantial proportion of Black
women and women of color, shelter-based housing interventions disproportionately affect these
populations nationally; and the challenged practices govern access to shelter exits, housing
stability, and the 8 women and their children affected by OHS’s practices were
disproportionately Black and women of color.
8. Whether the totality of the evidence supports a reasonable basis to believe that the
administration of federally funded housing programs by OHS may have violated Title VI
or related nondiscrimination requirements.
Based on the totality of the evidence, the investigation finds that there is a probable cause to
believe that OHS’s administration of federally-funded housing programs did not comply with
Title VI requirements.
9

Metro Government of Nashville and Davidson County, Tennessee - Code of Ordinances Title 2 - ADMINISTRATION Division I. - Council, Offices, Officers and Departments  Chapter 2.63 - OFFICE OF HOMELESS SERVICES
2.62.070 - Enforcement.
Division II. - Boards and Commissions
Chapter 2.63 - OFFICE OF HOMELESS SERVICES
2.63.010 - Creation.
There is hereby created an office of homeless services, which shall consist of a director and other such officers and employees as may be deemed necessary by the director.
(Ord. BL2021-971 § 1, 2022)
2.63.020 - Duties of office.
The duties of the office of homeless services shall include, but not limited to, the following: (1) providing expertise and coordinate a community response to homelessness including the management of emergency sheltering, coordinated entry, and the homeless management information system (HMIS); (2) providing resources and outreach regarding homelessness throughout Nashville and Davidson County; (3) providing staff and resources for the Metropolitan Homelessness Commission and the Nashville Davidson County Continuum of Care Homelessness Planning Council; and (4) maintaining an inventory of direct supportive services provided by third-party organizations to homeless populations to ensure that all areas of Davidson County are adequately served provided that (a) any publication or production of such information contain prominently displayed language stating that none of the providers listed therein or thereon have been vetted, verified, reviewed or approved by the office of homeless services; and (b) nothing provided herein shall be construed as a requirement that providers register with the office of homeless services.
(Amdt. 1 to Ord. BL2024-390 § 1, 2024; Ord. BL2024-390 § 1, 2024; Ord. BL2021-971 § 1, 2022)
2.63.030 - Personnel.
All employees of the Homeless Impact Division of Metropolitan Social Services shall be transferred to the office of homeless services.
(Ord. BL2021-971 § 1, 2022)
2.63.040 - Director.
The director of the office of homeless services shall be appointed by the mayor and, if appropriate, subject to the civil service provisions of this Charter. The department of human resources shall include at least one representative of the Nashville Davidson County Continuum of Care Homeless Planning Council in the interview and evaluation process. The chair of the homeless planning council shall recommend the individual from the Homeless Planning Council to participate in the process.
(Amdt. 2 to Ord. BL2021-971 § 1, 2022; Amdt. 1 to Ord. BL2021-971 § 1, 2022; Ord. BL2021-971 § 1, 2022)
